title: Kyle Williams, Patriots WRs Stand Out in Lopsided Offensive Performance
full_text:
FOXBORO — All summer, the chatter was about how deep the New England Patriots' wide receivers were . Adding A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs would help unlock a different part of this offense we didn't see a season ago.
But four weeks into the year, we really never got to mention DeMario Douglas or Kyle Williams a whole lot. Hell, before Efton Chism's heroics in Buffalo , he was rarely brought up. But now that Mack Hollins went down with a calf injury, all three of those players were crucial parts of the team's success in Week 5.
Douglas got the scoring started early in the Patriots' 45-17 beatdown of the Las Vegas Raiders , sprinting untouched for an opening 25-yard touchdown catch. Williams tacked on a team-high 91 yards after making a 34-yard touchdown grab of his own . Douglas would find the end zone once more in the final minutes of the fourth quarter. Chism was targeted the most out of any pass catcher (six) and caught five of them for 57 yards.
It was a great day for a room that only had four players suit up at kickoff.
"They're all ready to go. They all played different positions. That's not easy, you know, to learn three different positions and being able to step in there and block and make plays," Mike Vrabel said postgame. "The ball found each and every one of them. And I think (wide receivers coach) Todd (Downing) does a great job, and I think they all care about each other.
"Those receivers, they, they don't care who catches the ball. They don't care who catches a touchdown. They're just as excited for the next guy if it was them, and I think that that's truly what we wanna build around here, you know? And I gotta get it to be the entire team. I gotta get the entire team to look at it like that."
Downing, in his second year with the team, has preached "serving" in the meetings — and that was on display today.
"I feel like that's what God put us on this earth to do," Douglas said. "To serve others. And man, I feel like our group has been harping on that."
Part of their outing was the emergence of the true Drake Maye, who racked up five total touchdowns today in his first 300-yard game since December of last season . When the quarterback is firing on all cylinders, it helps out the wide receivers who might be playing in larger roles than they might have a year ago.
Maye was very complimentary of them.
"I'm confident in myself and my abilities and the guys around me," the quarterback said, who also connected with Hunter Henry for his own first touchdown of the season.
That group might not have had the largest external expectations coming into this game against a Raiders team that had more wins. But inside their locker room, those receivers knew what they were capable of.
"It's just how much respect we have for everyone's work ethic on a day-to-day basis," Chism said in front of his locker. "We all love each other. We're a tight group, and so I love seeing Kyle score, Rome score, Pop. It's just awesome. And with Mack and A.J. out — everyone is just so close and tight. It's an awesome room and I'm very blessed to be a part of it."
"We have a lot of talent. Everybody can do everything in that room," Williams said. "So when you gave a room like that, it's kind of easy. When people go down for them to step up because it's like we already know what they come with. And the preparation. ... It's not even a question what we did out there. It's not even a question of why it happened or how it happened because the preparation is what led us here today."
The Patriots will have the opportunity to get Brown back off of IR this week after his four-week hiatus. Adding that weapon into this receiving room should work wonders for this passing attack as it starts to find its groove.

title: Banged-Up Patriots Defense Answers the Call in Dominant Victory
full_text:
FOXBORO — When you look at the scoreboard following the New England Patriots' 45-17 drubbing of the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday , most thoughts will go straight to the offense. And deservingly so.
They scored seven times and Drake Maye had one of the best games of his career . And yet, the New England defense, one that sacked Kirk Cousins a season-high three times, stole the show. They were able to pressure the Raiders all afternoon and really limit anything past the first two drives of the game.
"It was a good win at home, and we just continue to build," edge rusher Gabe Jacas told Patriots On SI postgame. "We know we could utilize Kirk Cousins, him not being that mobile. We just know we ha fto affect the middle of the pocket. ... We just gave to win early and win early in the pocket."
The Raiders drove six plays for 66 yards early the first quarter, eventually tying the game up at seven on a Brock Bowers touchdown. But then they weren't able to get anything cooking. Their next two drives were punts, and then once they were gifted a fumble in Patriots territory, a doinked field goal from Matt Gay ended that chance for points.
All afternoon, the Patriots flew around the field. Christian Elliss led the team with seven tackles. Elijah Ponder had a pair of sacks, while Leonard Taylor III added another. Kindle Vildor ( who was just signed to the 53-man roster this weekend ) forced a fumble. The defense was swarming, and it allowed the offensive side of the ball to thrive without much pressure.
Las Vegas only mustered 38 yards on the ground (27 from Ashton Jeanty), and so that forced the ball to go in the air a lot more. Then the Patriots sent the hounds.
"They did a great job in their blitz package," Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak said. "When you pass it that many times, there's going to be those. But overall, I think they did a great job of pressuring us today."
When the defense gets to the quarterback and makes life difficult, that is a recipe for success.
"We wanted to heat him up a little bit, so we started to blitz and do some things like that," Kevin Byard said. "I think (defensive coordinator) Zak (Kuhr) called a great game."
The defense hasn't been the problem all season . But this week, no one would have faulted them considering how banged up they were. Entering Sunday, four (four!) cornerbacks were down for the count. Christian Gonzalez was out with a shoulder injury, Carlton Davis' neck injury flared up again and rookies Karon Prunty and Channing Canada both had hamstring ailments. Nobody would have batted an eye if a depleted secondary got carved up.
But they did step up. Sure, Bowers (eight receptions, 110 yards, one touchdown) was Bowers. But the team adjusted and started to close the gap.
They stood tough, albeit agianst not that great of a receiving room on the other side of the field. Tre Tucker led all Raiders wide receivers with four receptions for 41 yards. The next most? Cody White's two receptions for 44 yards. It was as shutdown as you can get when it comes to New England's corners against the Raiders' wideouts.
"I don't think you ever expect this, but I think there was a lot of respect for their defense, and I played here last year and didn't play, but preparing for them last season and watching their run to the Super Bowl, I think you saw an elite defense that was a Super Bowl caliber defense," Cousins said. "Felt that all week as we were preparing for this game, just that we were playing a very, very good defense."
Without their top cornerbacks , the team still got valuable snaps out of their trio of healthy cornerbacks ... at least for the time being. Marcus Jones stepped up, even though he was tasked with covering Bowers early in the game. Vildor shined, and Woods — who left the game early with a shoulder injury — played in a lot of two-cornerback sets. For how banged up they were, this unit was excellent.
"I was able to go out there and just execute the game plan that got for us," Vildor told Patriots On SI, who said that he knew all week he'd been ready for this game.
The Patriots are back with a winning record, and depending on how Monday Night Football unfolds with the Buffalo Bills, could be back in first place of the AFC East. This defensive performance will be one that the team can hang their hat on going into the fall months.
Mike Vrabel, though, knows that this win will only take them so far.
"Today's not gonna matter here in about 10 minutes," he said. "We're gonna have to focus on the Jets in the division here at home. We still have a lot to improve and to clean up."
Based on how the defense looked this week, you best believe that the sky still remains the limited for this group.

title: Patriots' Drake Maye Provides Stellar Performance in 45-17 Win Over Las Vegas
full_text:
The New England Patriots (3-2) beat the Las Vegas Raiders by a score of 45-1 7, behind an impressive performance from Drake Maye (371 yards, four passing touchdowns, one rushing touchdown).
Maye, who threw seven interceptions entering Sunday’s game against the Raiders, carried the Pats to their second-straight win. It was an efficient day for the 24-year-old, who completed 26 of his 34 pass attempts en route to his second game ever with more than 300 passing yards.
Topping Las Vegas in a dominant four-score victory, Maye has proven the the Patriots are ready to compete, especially because they have the 27th-easiest schedule remaining in the NFL.
Maye recorded four passing touchdowns in Sunday's victory, connecting with Hunter Henry, Kyle Williams, and Demario Douglas (who caught two). This bring his season passing total to eight touchdowns, doubling his previous recorded passing touchdown in 2026. Maye threw for four TDs during the first four weeks and threw the same amount in Week 5.
Maye also accounted for the Patriots second rushing touchdown of the game, scrambling to his left for a four-yard touchdown in the third quarter.
After a stroke of luck, Maye led the New England Patriots to a Super Bowl appearance in the 2025 season. Entering Sunday after a 2-2 start to the 2026 season, Maye and the Patriots look to improve on last year’s February loss to the Seattle Seahawks.
Following a 29-26 victory against division opponent Buffalo Bills and now this win, Maye has teased his potential as one of the NFL’s best young quarterbacks .
On Sunday, Maye threw for zero interceptions for the first time this season. His turnover tendency has defined his third-year as a professional, leaving many to wonder whether or not he regresses in 2026.
Entering Week 5, Maye recorded 11 turnovers in the Patriots' two wins and equal amount of losses. Having an almost-perfect game, with a 150.9 passer rating, the starting quarterback and his offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels have proven that they’ll be protecting the ball in future games to come.
A year ago, Drake Maye threw for 4,394 yards and 31 touchdowns. The runner-up MVP to Rams QB Matthew Stafford put the league on notice with his impressive second year campaign, throwing for 374 yards and scoring five total touchdowns.
With an underwhelming start to the season, many counted out Drake Maye and the Pats , but after grabbing a 3-2 record, the Patriots have once again emerged as an AFC contender.
Maye and the Pats will prepare for division opponent New York Jets (2-3) next Sunday in Foxborough.

title: 7 Takeaways From Patriots' Monster Win over Raiders: Is Drake Maye Finally Back?
full_text:
FOXBORO — It was a perfect day in New England . For the Patriots, everything from the pregame festivities to the performance on the field, was just the best possible situation. They also could put a winning record next to their name for the first time in 2026.
Fans at Gillette Stadium were treated to a 25th anniversary celebration of the Patriots' first Super Bowl team from 2001 and Adam Vinatieri's Pro Football Hall of Fame ring ceremony.
In between the lines, Drake Maye led the Patriots offense on six scoring drives en route to a 45-17 beatdown of the Las Vegas Raiders. Both sides combined for 217 penalty yards, but Maye's 399 total yards (374 of them through the air) were the catalyst for the Patriots' third win of the season.
Here's what happened, and what it means moving forward:
The Patriots entered the game with a limited bunch of wide receivers. Only four were active for kickoff (Romeo Doubs, Efton Chism III, Kyle Williams and DeMario Douglas), and out of that group, only Doubs and Chism had found the end zone prior to the game.
Under four minutes in, Douglas was able to add his name to that list. Aided by a long defensive pass interference penalty, Drake Maye got all the time in the world against a four-man rush. Douglas got wide open on a post out of the left slot, and was all alone in the end zone. Easy pitch-and-catch for the 35-yard score. Douglas would add another easy score late in the fourth quarter.
A Kirk Cousins-to-Brock Bowers tied the game up almost immediately on the following drive, but the Patriots would respond. A pair of fourth-down conversions to Douglas and Hunter Henry would set the table for the Patriots to reclaim it.
Rhamondre Stevenson powered his way in for a five-yard touchdown and the 14-7 lead. With the run, he became the eighth player in franchise history to record 30+ rushing touchdowns in his Patriots career.
Maye threw the ball in the direction of Doubs five times in the win. All of them came past the sticks. Doubs finished the day with just one reception for 16 yards, but solidified himself as the go-to threat down the sideline.
On the Patriots' first drive of the game, Doubs was targeted deep on the right side, but Raiders cornerback Eric Stokes was flagged for a 24-yard defensive pass interference. One drive later, Maye tried to hit Doubs again, but Stokes was called again for a 27-yard penalty. He'd be targeted again on the third drive, but had the ball batted out his hands by Raiders cornerback Darien Porter.
The Patriots had to place fullback Reggie Gilliam and wide receiver Mack Hollins on IR this week after injuries they suffered in the win over the Buffalo Bills. In the first half against Las Vegas, they lost two more offensive stars .
After multiple touches on their third drive of the game (including a fun trick play that saw Chism throw it to Henderson), the second-year running back departed to the locker room. He'd be announced as questionable to return with an ankle injury, and later downgraded to out.
On that same drive, starting left tackle Will Campbell would go down to the ground grabbing his right knee. He'd depart to the locker room and would be replaced by rookie Caleb Lomu. Campbell did not return after suffering a knee injury, and Lomu remained in the game.
In the second half, Charles Woods — who was limited all week in practice with a shoulder injury — blew up a screen pass to Bowers and stayed on a knee after the play. The cornerback would go into the blue medical tent and wouldn't return. Dre'Mont Jones and Cory Durden would also leave the game after being checked out on the field.
After Henderson left the game, the Patriots turned to third-string Corey Kiner to help with the rushing attack. But they didn't get much help out of the gate.
The second-year back fumbled his first carry of the game after it was punched out by Raiders defensive tackle (and former Patriots undrafted free agent) Adam Butler in the gap. The Raiders took over in prime position, but Matt Gay would doink a 49-yard field goal off the left upright.
Kiner would finish the game carrying the ball a few more times in a reserve role, including a 32-yard scamper in garbage time. An 11-yard touchdown to Hunter Henry would give the Patriots a 21-7 lead heading into halftime, ultimately wiping away Kiner's mistake.
Coming into the game, second-year edge rusher Elijah Ponder led the Patriots with 2.5 sacks . A little more than four hours later, Ponder added a pair to his year-long total. Ponder brought down Cousins twice — including a strip-sack to close the first half.
His ascend off the edge helped the Patriots defense hold a Raiders offense to just seven points (and hold them scoreless after their first drive of the game). It was his first multi-sack game of Ponder's young career.
Through the first four games of the season, the wide receiver had just two receptions for 44 yards. He'd surpass that level of production against the Raiders by a lot.
After Williams and Hezekiah Masses traded pass interference penalties, Maye dialed up a deep ball for his receiver down the left sideline. The speedster beat the rookie Masses from the first step and brought in the 34-yard score. That was the Patriots' fourth touchdown of the game. It wouldn't end there.
Following a Gay field goal, Maye would go on a surgical drive down the field. He hit Eli Raridon deep for a large pickup, used his legs to avoid a sack and then took a quarterback sweep behind the left side of the line for a three-year rushing score.
Williams would later tack on a 49-yard snag to close the third quarter on a drive ending with an Andy Borregales field goal. The Raiders would put in first overall pick Fernando Mendoza for his NFL debut late trailing by four scores.
It was a vintage (as vintage as a third-string quarterback can possibly play) showing from Maye, who ended his day completing 26-of-34 passes and racked up a 144.6 rating. He recorded back-to-back games with at least three touchdowns for the first time in his career, and it as the first time a Patriots quarterback did it since Tom Brady in 2018.
It was also the second time Maye surpassed 300 yards in the air in his career. Those 374 yards are just second to his 380 he had in Baltimore a season ago. The 24-year-old is now up to eight total touchdowns this season, and seven in his last two games. It's safe to say he's back.

title: Patriots Week 5 Inactives vs. Raiders: Secondary Taking Hit after Hit
full_text:
FOXBORO — The New England Patriots are sitting at 2-2, but it's taken some crazy turns to get them to that point . Bad losses, thrilling wins and a myriad of injuries have them back at home for a date with the Las Vegas Raiders.
But they won't be taking the field at full strength.
Here are all the players on the Patriots and Raiders that won't be suiting up for the Week 5 game:
QB Behren Morton (emergency third QB)
QB Aidan O'Connell (emergency third QB)
CB Christian Gonzalez (shoulder)
WR Jalen Nailor (concussion)
CB Karon Prunty (hamstring)
CB Channing Canada (hamstring)
The biggest story is Gonzalez and Davis sidelined once again . Gonzalez, who looked like he got banged up on a tackle in Week 3, told reporters after the game that he felt "good." But it's clear that he's dealing with something more serious than initially thought.
One big return will be Christian Barmore, who missed last week with a shoulder injury. He was questionable to play ( along with Rhamondre Stevenson ), but they will be out there.
Morton will only be allowed to play if both Drake Maye and Tommy DeVito get hurt. Practice squad elevation safety Elliott Davison will make his NFL debuts today. Linebacker K.J. Britt (practice squad) and safety Brenden Schooler (non-football injury list) will also make their season debuts.
Gonzalez missed last week, but it didn't seem like this injury — at least to me — would stretch into multiple weeks. Nope, the 24-year-old has missed six-straight practices and won't be dressing.
But it's not just Gonzalez who can't go. Davis, the Patriots' most physical cornerback at the line of scrimmage, is dealing with a neck injury that held him out of the team's Week 2 win against Pittsburgh. And then Karon Prunty and Channing Canada, both rookies, will miss the game with hamstring ailments.
To help fill the void at cornerback, the Patriots signed Kindle Vildor off of the practice squad to the 53-man roster . But that only brings the total active corners to three for the game.
The Patriots are rolling into the game with Vildor, Marcus Jones and Charles Woods (who entered the day questionable with a shoulder injury). I don't see the Raiders using their wide receivers a lot this game, so it might not be that big of a worry for New England. But this is easily the weakest part of the roster right now.
The Patriots are going to be without A.J. Brown for at least one more game, and then they had to put Mack Hollins on injured reserve with a calf injury . That leaves them with just four active wide receivers for the game (Kyle Dixon, Chandler Brayboy or Cameron Dorner weren't elevated off of the practice squad).
So it will be Romeo Doubs, Efton Chism III, DeMario Douglas and Kyle Williams this week. Chism, who was the hero in Buffalo for his game-winning touchdown snag , could see an uptick in snaps compared to the start of the year. He was the one to helped step up for Hollins after the vet went down.
“It wouldn’t be right for me to sit up here and not talk about his work ethic and his character," offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels said this week. "Since the moment we got him, he has been at the highest level. It’s hard to say that an undrafted college free agent would be a pros pro, but I will tell you that’s what he is. He came in with that kind of demeanor, that kind of attitude. He understands that I’m going to be ready when my time is up, and he was and has been since he’s been here."
If Drake Maye and the Patriots want to stack wins for the first time this season, they'll need one of these wideouts to really break out. Doubs and Chism both found the end zone last week, but Douglas and Williams are due for a stellar outing.
The Patriots and Raiders will kick off from Gillette Stadium at 1 p.m. EST. It's going to be a fun one in Foxboro, as the Patriots plan to honor the 25th anniversary of their Super Bowl XXXVI-winning team before the game . At halftime, they'll also give recent Pro Football Hall of Fame inductee Adam Vinatieri his induction ring — the first Patriots player to receive it since Richard Seymour in 2022. This week will also be the first of two times this season that the Patriots break out their Pat Patriot red throwback jerseys.

title: Social Media Rips Saints After Loss to Vikings, Lack of Homefield Advantage
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints' frustrating start to the 2026 season continued Sunday with a 23-13 loss to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings , dropping New Orleans to 1-4 and intensifying criticism surrounding second-year head coach Kellen Moore.
What was supposed to be a memorable afternoon celebrating Drew Brees' induction into the Saints Ring of Honor instead became another disappointing chapter in a season rapidly slipping away.
The Saints managed just 142 yards of total offense, while quarterback Tyler Shough struggled against Minnesota's relentless defensive pressure. Even an 87-yard fumble return touchdown by rookie safety Jonas Sanker wasn't enough to prevent New Orleans from suffering its fourth loss in five games.
The defeat also highlighted the Saints' deteriorating home-field advantage, with Vikings fans making their presence felt inside the Caesars Superdome.
As frustration continues to grow, three major talking points have emerged surrounding Moore's coaching, the defense's performance and the team's inability to protect its home field.
Of everyone facing criticism amid the New Orleans Saints' disappointing start, second-year head coach Kellen Moore has arguably received the most.
While Moore faced scrutiny throughout his first season, many fans remained patient, understanding that the franchise was undergoing a rebuild. However, that patience has steadily worn thin, particularly following the Saints' embarrassing loss to the Atlanta Falcons on the 20th anniversary of Domecoming .
The criticism reached a new level following Sunday's loss to Minnesota, marking New Orleans' third consecutive defeat, all coming inside the Caesars Superdome.
Much of the frustration centered on Moore's offensive play calling and his inability to make adjustments against Minnesota's relentless blitz packages.
Offensive sequences don't get much worse than this: MIN 46 1-10: Kendre Miller run (-1) MIN 47 2-11: Holding, Donaldson (-10) NO 43 2-21: False start (-5) NO 38 2-26: INT, Shough, plus, holding Kamara (-10, declined)
Even Saints legend Drew Brees questioned the predictability of Moore's offense during Fox's broadcast, further fueling criticism of the struggling head coach.
Drew Brees has been disgusted with Kellen Moore's play-calling all game. He's just dropping hints without bashing his franchise too hard.
The only reason Brees doesn’t really cut loose on this organization is because he doesn’t want to hurt Loomis or Gayle. But what he just said about our offense is probably the most blunt he can be without trying to offend them.
With New Orleans managing just 142 total yards, including 96 passing, questions continue to mount about Moore's offensive philosophy, game planning and ability to turn the franchise around.
What began as patience during a rebuilding process has increasingly turned into frustration, with fans questioning whether Moore is the right coach to lead the Saints into the future.
Someone threw out a great stat on my show last week.  Not a positive one but… The @Saints have a lower winning percentage post @drewbrees than before him arriving in New Orleans.  That includes the teams first 20 years of ineptness.  Last 5+ years, some lousy football. Not good
In Kellen Moore's 22 games with the #Saints : - 7-15, 3-8 at home. - Have never scored more than 7 in the 1st quarter. - 1 first-quarter lead. - 4 first-half leads. - Fewest 1st quarter points scored (35) - Most 1st quarter 3-and-outs (29) - Third-worst turnover margin (-10)
While the offense received much of the blame, the defense also drew scrutiny after allowing Minnesota to produce its most productive offensive performance of the season.
The Vikings finished with 364 total yards, including 153 rushing, while quarterback Kyler Murray threw for 229 yards and rushed for another 54.
Aaron Jones rushed for 113 yards and a touchdown, while Justin Jefferson added six receptions for 79 yards and a touchdown. He became the third player to rush for over 100 yards or more after Detroit's Jahmyr Gibbs and Atlanta's Bijan Robinson
This isn't the only bad performance as New Orleans allowed Atlanta to have over 420 yards, including 205 on the ground.
While they haven't allowed as many gaudy passing yards (because their opponents are having success running the ball), the Saints secondary isn't any better.
Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry has been a major liability in the Saints' secondary through five games, earning a dismal 55.6 overall Pro Football Focus (PFF) grade and an even worse 51.7 coverage grade. Opposing quarterbacks have completed 60.7% of their passes when targeting him, resulting in 255 yards and a touchdown, while McKinstry has yet to record an interception.
That has earned him the nickame "Sugar Water McKinstry" from ESPN 104.5 radio host Matt Moscona.
LMAO Matt Moscona called Kool-Aid McKinstry “Sugar Water McKinstry” 😭😭 ultimate slander name pic.twitter.com/H2r78MvHk4
Despite forcing two turnovers, including Sanker's fumble return touchdown, the Saints struggled to get Minnesota off the field in critical situations.
That scoop and score was the perfect embodiment of being a Saints fan since Brees has retired. The second you get excited and rejuvenated, they turn right around and kill your vibes.
The performance raised further questions about a defense that has struggled with consistency throughout the early season.
While the Saints’ defense surrendered season-high numbers to a weak Minnesota offense , Sunday's loss highlighted a bigger issue off the field: the Caesars Superdome has lost its elite home-field advantage.
Historically one of the NFL's toughest environments, the venue no longer intimidates visitors. New Orleans has dropped three of four home games this season and sits at 15-21 at home since coach Sean Payton left after 2021, with only one winning home season (5-3 in 2023). The collapse is even sharper recently, with 14 losses in their last 17 home games since 2024.
Compounding the loss, traveling Vikings fans filled the stands with loud "Skol" chants.
Fan frustration continues to grow alongside the home struggles, proving that restoring the Dome's advantage requires winning games, not just past reputation. Until Moore's team delivers, visiting crowds will remain right at home.
It’s bad pic.twitter.com/rrwsCU7nPV
For perspective on how many Vikings fans were in the Superdome today. There was a Saints third down late in the game that you might’ve thought this was a road game. Tough to put into words just how far down the sentiment around this season has fallen in the span of three weeks. pic.twitter.com/Ne8pCQBUDa
In a span of 7 days, you can hear audible ATL chants and SKOL chants. What this franchise has done to our Superdome since Brees retired should be punishable by crime.

title: Drew Brees Questions Kellen Moore's Offense as Saints' Struggles Continue Against Vikings
full_text:
During the second half of the New Orleans Saints' 23-13 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , franchise legend Drew Brees openly criticized head coach Kellen Moore 's offensive approach on a nationwide broadcast.
Working as a Fox analyst shortly after being inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor at halftime, Brees pointed to New Orleans' inability to adjust against Minnesota's relentless blitzing defense .
Specifically, Brees called the Saints' first-down play calling "pretty predictable," questioned the lack of play-action passes, and criticized setup choices that left running back Alvin Kamara in unfavorable matchups.
"You gotta have answers," Brees said, highlighting the team's ongoing struggles in front of a national audience.
Quarterback Tyler Shough suffered through the toughest game of his fledgling career as the Saints (1-4) were held to a paltry 142 total yards—their lowest output since Week 2 of 2021.
Preliminary charting from Pro Football Focus showed Minnesota bringing blitz pressure on 23 of Shough's 27 dropbacks. The second-year passer managed only 16 completions on 25 attempts for 96 yards, throwing two interceptions and posting a career-worst 38.1 passer rating.
Head coach Kellen Moore admitted the team's offensive strategy was ineffective against the Vikings' aggressive scheme.
"I felt like we had a plan (against the blitz)," Moore stated. "Obviously the plan wasn't good enough. They did a better job."
"Obviously, that's on me."
The offensive struggles stemmed from an inability to sustain early momentum and adapt late. New Orleans opened with a promising 15-play, 66-yard scoring drive capped by a 1-yard Kendre Miller touchdown run, but the rushing attack completely stalled afterward. Over their next six drives, the Saints generated a mere 10 yards on the ground as penalties and negative plays continually forced them into obvious passing downs.
A reluctance to adjust the play calling aggravated these issues down the stretch. According to FTN Fantasy, New Orleans entered the contest utilizing play action on just 17.7% of offensive snaps—the fourth-lowest rate in the NFL. Against Minnesota, they called only one play-action pass, which gained 14 yards to Chris Olave .
Special teams miscues and missed chances further doomed the Saints. Jayden Price lost a fumble on the second-half opening kickoff, while Daniel Carlson missed a point-after attempt following an 87-yard fumble return touchdown by Jonas Sanker .
The defense's takeaway went unrewarded, while Minnesota (5-0) anticipated the Saints' aerial concepts, as demonstrated by Byron Murphy intercepting Shough on a late double move intended for Olave.
"They were really prepared for those moments," Shough remarked.
With a 1-4 record through five games, Moore faces mounting criticism during a difficult start to his second year, as New Orleans struggles with preparation, execution, and identity.
"Sometimes, you go through storms," Moore acknowledged. "Inevitably, storms end. But we're going through a little bit of one."

title: Saints vs. Vikings: The Good, Bad and Ugly From New Orleans' 23-13 Loss
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints' struggles continued Sunday as they fell 23-13 to the Minnesota Vikings inside the Caesars Superdome.
The defeat dropped New Orleans to 1-4 for the second consecutive season, further exposing the growing problems facing second-year head coach Kellen Moore and a team that continues to take steps backward .
Here is the Good, Bad and Ugly from the Saints' 23-13 loss to the Vikings.
In one of the few bright spots in the loss to the Vikings, Saints 2nd year safety Jonas Sanker provided a game-changing spark by returning a fumble 88 yards for a touchdown to tie the game at 13-13 late in the second quarter.
Sanker's touchdown demonstrated that New Orleans still has young players capable of making an impact despite a disappointing 1-4 start, though Daniel Carlson subsequently missed the go-ahead extra point.
Fumble 🗣️ Jonas Sanker recovers and takes it to the end zone to tie it up! @MINvsNO on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/W52Ypr6gtT
The second-year defensive back has been tasked with helping rebuild a Saints defense that has undergone significant turnover, delivering an impressive defensive scoring play against Minnesota's undefeated squad.
Ultimately, the Saints' offense failed to capitalize on the momentum, leaving the defense with little margin for error as New Orleans dropped its fourth game of the season.
Shough has been the Saints’ best player throughout the season as he, along with a few others, is the bright spot on what is a bad football team at the moment and if it weren’t for him this season would be a complete disaster.
However, his performance was not good enough for New Orleans to win this game.
Shough had his worst game of the season, completing 16 of his 25 passes for only 96 yards and two interceptions. A lot of his struggles could be placed on the Vikings’ defense and their blitz packages, which present a lot of looks that could deceive a quarterback and his offensive line.
"It was obviously very difficult," Shough said of going up against Minnesota’s defense. "They presented a lot of looks. That's what they're extremely good at. I felt like we were ready for all those looks. We just didn't execute in some of those moments, and now we're second and 20, or third and 15, and — I mean, you're not — those odds are not really in your favor for those situations.
"And we got to be in those third-and-six, third-and-five, third-and-three ranges, where we can convert and dictate tempo. We had a couple good drives and moments, but I don't care who we're playing, we got to be better there. And especially against that team, they're really well coached, really played really well."
While the Saints’ defense allowed a putrid Minnesota offense to put up its best numbers of the season, the most concerning aspect of Sunday's defeat occurred off the field.
The game served as a stark reminder that the Caesars Superdome no longer offers the formidable environment it was once famous for.
Historically, New Orleans boasted one of the premier home-field advantages in the NFL, where deafening crowd noise and an unyielding Saints team made life miserable for visiting opponents.
That distinct edge appears to have vanished.
The Saints have lost all of their four home games this year (including preseason), extending a troubling pattern that began after former head coach Sean Payton left the team following the 2021 campaign.
Since Payton's departure, New Orleans has posted a sub-.500 record of 15-21 at home, managing just a single winning season in the Superdome (5-3 in 2023).
The situation has grown even more dire recently, as the Saints have dropped 14 of their last 17 home contests since the start of 2024.
Yet, the venue's atmosphere on Sunday was perhaps just as unsettling as the loss itself.
A massive contingent of traveling Vikings supporters made their presence felt, filling the Superdome with loud, distinct "Skol" chants.
For perspective on how many Vikings fans were in the Superdome today. There was a Saints third down late in the game that you might’ve thought this was a road game. Tough to put into words just how far down the sentiment around this season has fallen in the span of three weeks. pic.twitter.com/Ne8pCQBUDa
For an organization that built its reputation on creating a hostile environment for opponents, watching opposing fans dominate sections of the stadium underscored the team's ongoing decline.
Understandably, persistent losing eventually takes a toll on crowd enthusiasm and game-day attendance.
With little evidence of progress on the field, fan frustration continues to mount alongside the team's home struggles.
Reestablishing a true home-field advantage will require more than past glory or fan loyalty.
It must be reclaimed by winning football games.
Until Moore and the Saints deliver better results in front of their home crowd, visiting teams and their fans will continue to feel right at home in New Orleans.

title: Saints Must Accomplish 3 Things to End Minnesota's Perfect Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (1-3) enter Sunday's Week 5 matchup against the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings (4-0) looking to bounce back from a humbling 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night.
However, getting back on track won't be easy against a Minnesota team that has relied on one of the NFL's most dominant defenses to overcome its offensive struggles.
Sunday's matchup will also be a special occasion for the franchise as legendary quarterback Drew Brees will be inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor, adding even more significance to a game in which New Orleans desperately needs a victory.
For the Saints, the challenge will be giving their former quarterback and the home crowd something to celebrate while avoiding a third consecutive loss at the Caesars Superdome.
Doing so will require significant improvements on both sides of the ball, particularly against a Vikings defense that has consistently overwhelmed opposing offenses.
Here are three keys to victory for the Saints as they look to hand Minnesota its first loss of the season.
The Saints’ matchup against the Vikings will hinge on whether New Orleans can handle Minnesota’s league-leading blitz and pressure package. Minnesota enters Week 5 with arguably the NFL's best defense through four games, allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game while racking up 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-five turnover differential, the second-best mark in the league.
That is a major concern for a Saints offense that has struggled with consistency, protection, and turnovers. New Orleans has surrendered 12 sacks through four games, turned the ball over too often and enters Sunday with a minus-five turnover differential. Against a defense that thrives on disguising coverages, generating pressure from different alignments and forcing difficult decisions, the Saints cannot afford to fall behind early or repeatedly find themselves in obvious passing situations.
The biggest individual matchup is quarterback Tyler Shough against Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores ’ blitz-heavy system. Shough has already been sacked a dozen times this, with nine coming against the blitz, and New Orleans will need clear answers built into the game plan to avoid exposing him to the same issues again.
There are reasons for optimism. When Shough has gotten the ball out against blitzing defenses, he has been productive, posting a 105.1 passer rating while completing 71.9% of his passes and throwing for 442 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. But Minnesota has been uniquely effective at creating negative plays, and the Vikings’ No. 2 pressure rate will make life difficult if the Saints cannot keep the pocket clean.
Containing opposing top receivers has plagued the Saints through four games, making Sunday’s matchup against Vikings superstar Justin Jefferson a severe challenge.
Despite Minnesota ranking last in passing and 31st in total offense, Jefferson’s elite route-running, explosiveness, and contested-catch ability threaten New Orleans’ vulnerable secondary.
These defensive struggles were evident in Week 3 when Raiders tight end Brock Bowers posted 10 catches, 119 yards, and a touchdown from Kirk Cousins in Las Vegas' 31-28 win.
They continued Monday against Atlanta, as Drake London caught five passes for 96 yards, including a 37-yarder over Kool-Aid McKinstry , despite the Falcons leaning on the run.
New Orleans' secondary has struggled with missed tackles, blown coverages, penalties, and big plays.
Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. averaged 11.2 yards per attempt, going 15-for-20 for 223 yards and a touchdown.
Cornerbacks Quincy Riley (58 yards, TD allowed; 28.0 PFF grade) and McKinstry (60 yards allowed, two penalties; 29.5 PFF grade) were especially exploited.
These defensive flaws create major concerns facing Jefferson.
Unlike Bowers' versatile tight end mismatches or London's size, Jefferson combines route precision, speed, and versatility across alignments.
Leaving McKinstry or Riley isolated on Jefferson could prove disastrous for defensive coordinator Brandon Staley .
New Orleans must disguise coverages and offer safety help to force Kyler Murray elsewhere.
However, over-committing to Jefferson risks leaving tight end T.J. Hockenson (13 catches, 119 yards last week vs. Miami ) open underneath against an injured Saints linebacker corps.
Ultimately, New Orleans must force Minnesota into long, sustained drives without letting Jefferson dominate.
The four-game difference between these teams centers on protecting the football and capitalizing on errors.
Minnesota's plus-five turnover differential ranks tied for second-best in the NFL, whereas New Orleans ranks among the worst at minus-five. This 10-turnover gap clarifies how undefeated Minnesota overcomes an unproductive offense, while New Orleans loses despite averaging 367 yards and 26.3 points.
The Saints cannot afford to let turnovers, defensive breakdowns, and self-inflicted mistakes ruin offensive output against Minnesota's elite defense. Additionally, the Vikings lead the league in punt return average and rank second in kickoff return average, threatening a Saints squad already struggling with field position.
To succeed, New Orleans must secure the ball, limit penalties, convert in the red zone, force long drives, and avoid slow starts that play into Flores's pressure scheme. Even with Drew Brees honored at halftime and a supportive home crowd, emotional momentum will not offset repeated mistakes.

The New Orleans Saints will have their hands full Sunday when they welcome one of the NFL's remaining undefeated teams to the Caesars Superdome.
Coming off a 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night, New Orleans (1-3) will look to avoid its fourth consecutive defeat against a Minnesota Vikings team that has emerged as one of the NFL's early surprises.
Minnesota enters Week 5 with a 4-0 record following a 15-10 victory over the Miami Dolphins. While the Vikings haven't necessarily overwhelmed opponents offensively, their defense has been among the league's best, and they've consistently found ways to win close games.
Under head coach Kevin O'Connell , Minnesota has relied on a combination of aggressive defense, timely offensive production and an ability to capitalize on opponents' mistakes.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Vikings heading into Sunday's matchup.
Sunday’s matchup between the Saints and Vikings will hinge on whether New Orleans can handle Minnesota’s league-leading blitz and pressure package. Minnesota enters Week 5 with arguably the NFL's best defense through four games, allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game while racking up 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-five turnover differential, the second-best mark in the league.
That is a major concern for a Saints offense that has struggled with consistency, protection and turnovers. New Orleans has surrendered 12 sacks through four games, turned the ball over too often and enters Sunday with a minus-five turnover differential. Against a defense that thrives on disguising coverages, generating pressure from different alignments and forcing difficult decisions, the Saints cannot afford to fall behind early or repeatedly find themselves in obvious passing situations.
The biggest individual matchup is quarterback Tyler Shough against Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores ’ blitz-heavy system. Shough has already been sacked 12 times this season, with nine coming against the blitz, and New Orleans will need clear answers built into the game plan to avoid exposing him to the same issues again.
There are reasons for optimism. When Shough has gotten the ball out against blitzing defenses, he has been productive, posting a 105.1 passer rating while completing 71.9% of his passes and throwing for 442 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. But Minnesota has been uniquely effective at creating negative plays, and the Vikings’ No. 2 pressure rate will make life difficult if the Saints cannot keep the pocket clean.
New Orleans (1-3) will need to rely on a game plan that can sustain those positive trends under pressure. Without much help from the rushing attack, the Saints must produce through the air to pull out their first home win, and Minnesota is built to complicate exactly that.
A key question for Sunday's game is whether Minnesota All-Pro receiver Justin Jefferson will play.
Jefferson, who has 13 catches for 179 yards and two touchdowns in three games, is recovering from a Week 3 ankle injury. After missing last week's game against Miami, he returned to practice on a limited basis and has been listed as questionable for Sunday’s game.
With a bye following Sunday's game, Minnesota is evaluating whether to rest Jefferson to allow additional recovery time before Oct. 25, according to head coach Kevin O'Connell.
The Vikings face other offensive injury concerns: receiver Jordan Addison (hamstring) and tackle Brian O'Neill are also questionable, while tackle Christian Darrisaw will miss the game.
Jefferson's absence would aid a struggling Saints secondary, though Minnesota still retains offensive threats like tight end T.J. Hockenson .
Despite being undefeated, the Vikings have averaged just 21.5 points (18th in the NFL) and 263 yards per game.
Quarterback Kyler Murray has 433 passing yards, one touchdown and two interceptions. Running back Aaron Jones leads Minnesota with 297 rushing yards, while tight end T.J. Hockenson leads the team with 22 catches for 195 yards and one score.
In their 15-10 win over Miami, the Vikings did not score a single touchdown, highlighting their reliance on defense.
If New Orleans can contain Jones, limit Murray and force long third downs, it will have a chance to keep the game competitive. However, the Saints must still score against a formidable Minnesota defense to avoid another loss.

title: Saints vs. Vikings: Week 5 Staff Predictions and Final Score Picks
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (1-3) enter Sunday's Week 5 matchup against the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings (4-0) looking to bounce back from an embarrassing 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night.
However, getting back on track won't be easy against a Minnesota team that has relied on one of the NFL's most dominant defenses to overcome its offensive struggles.
Sunday's matchup will also be a special occasion for the franchise, as legendary quarterback Drew Brees will be inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor, giving New Orleans a chance to celebrate one of the greatest players in team history.
For the Saints, the challenge will be giving their former quarterback and the home crowd something to celebrate while avoiding a third consecutive loss at the Caesars Superdome. It also serves as an important test for second-year head coach Kellen Moore and a team still searching for consistency on both sides of the ball.
Can the Saints respond to Monday's humiliation and win on Brees' special day, or will the Vikings' suffocating defense spoil the celebration and keep Minnesota unbeaten?
Here's how we think Sunday's matchup will unfold, along with our final score predictions.
Which Saints team is going to show up? The one that put up a fight against Detroit, Las Vegas, and Baltimore, or the one that was taken to the woodshed by their rivals, the Falcons on Monday?
I know people talk about must-win situations, but for me this is more of a test: a test of leadership of this 2026 team.
Tyler Shough, Cam Jordan, Chase Young , and others all say the right thing. Shough talks about it being a bad game for them, and they've got to do better. Jordan used an expletive after the game to express his disgust. Young is not a happy camper either. But if their fellow squad members aren't heeding these leaders' revulsion for Monday's results, they may as well be in an empty echo chamber.
The man at the top is where it starts. I know the Saints are in a rebuilding process that will take a while, but what happened Monday on their home turf is something coach Kellen Moore cannot tolerate. Since we only see snippets of practice sessions, I cannot tell you what Moore has said or hasn't said to his troops. If we go by what we see on the sidelines and in interviews, I do not think the fire-breathing dragon type of coach some are asking for will magically materialize. I think what you see is what you're getting.
So, this test of leadership begins against an unbeaten Minnesota team Sunday whose defense DOES play like their hair is on fire, the way we all thought the Saints would be on Monday against those darn Falcons. Will the leaders of this Saints team make a statement? Will the rest of the squad follow the marching orders they are given?
After two straight home losses, I cannot say this team has proven it will.
This is a matchup I do not like one bit for the Saints.
Sunday’s Saints-Vikings game hinges on New Orleans handling Minnesota’s league-leading pressure. The Vikings’ top-ranked defense allows a league-low 12.8 points per game with 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-5 turnover differential.
This poses a major challenge for a struggling Saints offense that has allowed 12 sacks and holds a minus-5 turnover differential. New Orleans cannot afford to fall behind against Minnesota's disguised coverages and pressure scheme.
The crucial key is quarterback Tyler Shough facing Minnesota defensive coordinator Brian Flores ’ blitz-heavy scheme. Nine of Shough’s 12 sacks have come against blitzes. While he has excelled when throwing against the blitz—posting a 105.1 passer rating with four touchdowns and one interception—Minnesota's No. 2 pressure rate will test New Orleans’ pass protection.
With minimal ground support, New Orleans (1-3) must succeed through the air under constant pressure to secure its first home win.
Unlike the previous four teams they have faced, Minnesota’s offense is quite terrible despite its 4-0 start.
The Vikings have averaged a league-worst 4.4 yards per play and rank last in passing offense, averaging 156 yards per game and ranking 31st in offensive success rate. They've also managed to win two games without scoring an offensive touchdown, including last week's 15-10 victory over Miami, when all 15 points came from kicker Will Reichard.
Quarterback Kyler Murray and Minnesota's offense have struggled to consistently sustain drives, and the uncertainty surrounding Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison could make matters worse. Both receivers entered the weekend listed as questionable.
However, Aaron Jones is still a solid back at 31 years old, and if Jefferson can play Sunday, it would be a major boost to this Minnesota offense.
However, I think Minnesota does enough defensively to win the game.

title: Giants Notebook: Harbaugh on Run Defense, Injuries, Purple Hearts and Bryan Hudson
full_text:
The silver lining amid the dark clouds of the New York Giants ’ Week 5 tie with the Washington Commanders is that Big Blue increased its lead over the rest of the division by a half game.
Still, a win would have been nicer.
“I told the guys, ‘Was it a win?’ No. ‘Was it a loss?’ No. It was a tie,” head coach John Harbaugh said after the game on Sunday. “‘How does that make you feel?’ I’m happy it wasn’t a loss, and I’m sad it wasn’t a win. So that’s how I feel. It’s a tie. It’s a heck of a lot better than a loss, but it’s not as good as a win.”
But as with any game, the coaches and players gained additional insight into what they did well and what they didn’t.
For example, the Giants appear to have found the right formula to bring out the best in quarterback Jameis Winston when New York switched to more of a drop-back passing attack.
“It was good, no question. We’ve been talking about some of the tempo stuff,” Harbaugh said. “We’ve been working on that. It’s been part of our system from day one, really. It’s something we built in from the beginning. And it was good to get to it. We’ve been talking about getting to it. We got to it maybe because we had to.
“So yeah, it opened up the offense. It was good to see, and it probably needs to be part of what we’re doing going forward.”
And then there was the “feast or famine” nature of the run defense, which was gouged for 202 yards by the Commanders, the fourth-highest rushing total of Week 5.
“I think we’ve had too many chunk plays overall,” he said. “We’ve had a lot of really good plays, a lot of really good plays in that game where we stuffed the run, which we’re very capable of doing. And then there are a couple of line of scrimmage runs that get out on us that we’re not happy about that can be played so much better.”
Harbaugh said that pre-snap motion is part of the problem.
“Whether we don’t adjust to a motion the right way, we don’t get over in our gaps, we don’t quite come in through the angles,” he said.
“I think sometimes our tackling in the back end is really good. And sometimes it’s not good, especially if it’s spacey. It’s always tough to tackle a really fast ball carrier, especially a scrambling quarterback who can run in man coverage. And that’s what they caught us in.”
Here are three other things we learned from Harbaugh’s Monday video call with the media.
The Giants came out of the game with injuries to three key players: right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), safety Tyler Nubin (neck), and cornerback Colton Hood (concussion).
“Yeah, the three main guys are going to be day-to-day this week,” Harbaugh said. “They’ll have a chance for the game. We’ll have to see how it goes throughout the course of the week.”
Cornerback Greg Newsome II was also banged up in the game, though the nature of his injury isn’t known. But Harbaugh didn’t see Newsome’s ailment as one that might keep him out of practice this week, saying that the cornerback “was fine.”
Harbaugh did not offer any updates on safety Jason Pinnock, who missed Sunday’s game with a concussion suffered in the win over Arizona. Pinnock is thought to have traveled with the team to Washington, which would suggest he may be further along in the protocol.
Harbaugh also didn’t want to say whether cornerback Paulson Adebo, who now eligible to have his 21-day practice window opened, would be back at practice this week.
Harbaugh has implemented a merit-based patch system in which players are recognized for superlative efforts with a patch that’s stitched to their practice jerseys. Previously reported patches have rewarded players for meeting a percentage of offseason program attendance and for having played in the postseason as Giants.
He has added a “Purple Heart” patch to the collection. “It’s one of our awards for guys that are working through injury-type things, that they play, or they come back from,” he said.
He revealed that receiver Malik Nabers received a Purple Heart in Week 1, and offensive lineman Andrew Thomas, who has been battling a groin issue over the last several weeks, was a recent recipient.
“I think he’s doing a really good job of just playing through whatever he’s got,” Harbaugh said.
“Guys have things this time of year. He’s doing a great job. He’s so tough. Got the Purple Heart last week. He’s playing at a high level. I mean, it may be laboring for him, but still the result is better than almost every player in the league at that position.”
Harbaugh confirmed that Bryan Hudson will remain the team’s starting center for the upcoming game against the New Orleans Saints.
Harbaugh, who generally doesn’t like to reveal personnel plans, praised Hudson, who has now started two games in place of John Michael Schmitz.
Hudson has allowed just one pressure in 102 pass-blocking snaps , and is PFF’s second-highest-graded Giants offensive lineman in pass blocking, behind Eluemunor.
Hudson has really stood out in run-blocking, where his 72.3 run-blocking grade is the best among Giants offensive linemen this season.
“He played well in the game the week before, and he played well in this past game,” Harbaugh said. “Things he can do better, but things he did really well, and that’s what we based it on.”
The Giants head coach added that Schmitz is still in the plans. However, Harbaugh didn’t specify whether he meant the offense or special teams, where Schmitz contributed in Week 5 against the Commanders. Schmitz did not play in Week 4 against the Cardinals despite being active.

title: Giants Add Dawuane Smoot to Practice Squad Amid Run Defense Concerns
full_text:
The New York Giants continued their search for defensive line help on Monday by signing defensive lineman Dawuane Smoot to their practice squad.
Per the league’s transaction wire, Smoot had been in for a visit, while fellow defensive linemen Julian Okwara and Yannick Ngakoue were both in for tryouts.
Smoot is a 10-year NFL veteran who entered the league as a third-round pick in 2017. The 31-year-old has played in 127 games with 21 career starts and has 27 sacks.
Smoot, 6-foot-3 and 275 pounds, spent the 2024 season with Buffalo before returning to the Jaguars in 2025.
The Giants have been on a nonstop hunt for defensive line help, focusing on depth behind starters Shelby Harris and D.J. Reader. The Giants’ run defense, in particular, has been inconsistent all season, with the unit running hot and cold.
This past weekend, it ran cold, allowing 202 rushing yards on 30 carries (6.7 avg.) to the Washington Commanders in its Week 5 27-27 overtime tie.
That performance means the Giants’ run defense has allowed 638 total rushing yards, tied for sixth most in the league with Green Bay. And the Giants, who have allowed 5.2 yards per carry to opponents, are tied with the Raiders for second in that category.
“I think we’ve had too many chunk plays overall,” head coach John Harbaugh said of the run defense during his Monday video call.
“We’ve played a kind of feast or famine run defense. We’ve had a lot of really good plays, a lot of really good plays in that game where we stuffed the run, which we’re very capable of doing.
“And then there are a couple of line of scrimmage runs that get out on us that we’re not happy about that can be played so much better. Whether we don’t adjust to a motion the right way, we don’t get over in our gaps, we don’t quite come in through the angles.”
To Harbaugh’s point, the Giants are tied for the seventh-most big-play runs allowed (17) with Arizona and Detroit. The Giants are also tied for the fourth-most rushing plays allowed of 20 or more yards with six.
Reader (53%) and Harris (49%) have handled most of the run defense’s snaps up front, but the dropoff has been most evident behind them.
So the Giants have been trying to find the right blend of backup depth to help fortify their first line of run defense, a process that’s been ongoing even before the Giants traded Dexter Lawrence II earlier this year.

title: Giants Offense Grades: Winston, Nabers and Likely Rally in 27-27 Tie vs. Washington
full_text:
Jameis Winston threw for 326 yards and three touchdowns in the rain, but it wasn’t enough as the New York Giants escaped from Northwest Stadium with a 27-27 overtime tie against the Washington Commanders.
The Giants’ offense played a tale of two halves, managing just 77 net yards in the first half before the coaches shifted to a more drop-back approach after the break, which produced 240 net yards in the second half of regulation.
The second half also saw some of the Giants’ playmakers who had been nonfactors in the first 30 minutes come alive. Those included tight end Isaiah Likely, who contributed two touchdowns to help the Giants erase a 14-point deficit, and receiver Malik Nabers, who delivered the game-tying score with 1:43 left in the fourth quarter.
The Giants’ ground game remains an enigma, finishing with just 3.7 yards per carry as Washington committed to shutting down the run and forcing Winston to beat the Commanders through the air in sloppy, rainy conditions.
It wasn’t the win the Giants were hoping for, but the tie does increase their lead in the division to 1.5 games, a better outcome than a loss would have been.
Here is how each offensive player graded out against the Commanders, from the quarterbacks through the offensive line.
Winston has been this team’s starting quarterback for three weeks now, and each game has been a “weather” game. His offense has scored 12, 30, and 27 points. He should be 3-0 if not for Cam Skattebo’s backbreaking fumble.
After a slow start, Winston’s arm came alive, as he threw three touchdowns and no interceptions. He also threw for 326 yards on a day better suited for ducks.
After a very sluggish first half, in which the offense lost most every battle at the line of scrimmage, Winston came out on fire in the second half, and he did it without a running game.
Talk about clutch: all three of his touchdown throws came in that second half, the final one with 1:43 left in the fourth quarter to tie the game 27-27.
Admittedly, Winston contributed to the early-game mess with poor pocket awareness that led to the game’s two sacks. After his sack/fumble at the end of the first half, when he should have fallen on the ball instead of trying to pick it up, Winston wasn’t sacked a single time.
In the second half, the Giants seemed more aligned with what the Commanders’ defense was doing, and Winston started getting the ball out of his hands more quickly.
As for the deep ball, New York completed three of 11 attempts in that area. Until the deep ball plays a bigger role on offense, defenses will keep attacking the line of scrimmage and mucking up the running game.
All of McCarthy’s half-dozen snaps were gadget plays, and one drew a facemask penalty on Washington. His two runs went for two yards.
His lone pass was a receiver screen on which he showed off his fast release and strong arm; the completion to Nabers went for 14 yards, but an illegal shift nullified it.
It was interesting how the coaches forced him into the QB rotation so quickly. The coming weeks might be even more interesting, but only if Winston struggles.
It looked like Skattebo was running in place throughout a first half in which he had 12 yards on six carries and nothing through the air.
On the first possession of the second half, he had runs of 7 and 4 yards, his two longest runs of the day to that point. He also threw a couple of positive pass blocks, an area that needed to improve.
He didn’t get a single touch on that big third-quarter drive. In fact, he didn’t come alive until the second overtime series.
His 19-yard run on 3rd-and-2 on a wide toss was a nice change of pace, given how Washington had been packing it in between the tackles all game long.
Runs of 9 and 5 yards set up the offense at the two-minute warning, but on the very next snap, Skattebo allowed the ball to get punched out of his grasp for the backbreaking turnover. It was a great play by the defense, but his third fumble in five games should be setting off alarms in the Giants’ coaching room.
A lack of speed at the position is another big red flag this organization needs to address in the offseason.
Harris looked just as sluggish as the starter early on as the O-line could not sustain its blocks. Harris managed only nine yards on five carries and five yards on one reception in his rotation role.
The second half was a passing man’s paradise, which limited Harris’s playing time, and he was barely utilized throughout the fourth quarter and overtime.
Tracy also did not get much going from scrimmage this week, finishing with six yards on three carries. But his two catches for 25 yards should be a harbinger of things to come.
The Giants need a third-down back, and Tracy should have the job. For the last two weeks, his pass-blocking has been superb.
His fourth-down, 21-yard checkdown scamper was one of the second half’s bigger plays. It remains to be seen whether that will be enough for Tracy to start getting most of his snaps on passing downs.
It’s impressive that Nabers has topped 100 receiving yards the last two weeks, in bad weather no less. And yet people, or more specifically Nabers himself, are saying he doesn’t look like himself yet.
Yes, he’s returning from knee surgery, but he's really picked it up over the last two weeks, with 112 yards on six receptions last week and 121 yards on 11 receptions this week.
He scored a touchdown each week, including a clutch, deep middle route this week that tied the game at 27-27 late in the fourth quarter.
Nabers couldn’t get to one deep ball, and people are still waiting to see more explosiveness. He’s “killing it” in the intermediate areas, with his longest catch a 28-yarder in overtime that set up the offense for the game-winning field goal that never came.
He also had earlier receptions of 14, 16, 18, and 20 yards as he did what most secondaries do these days: keep things in front of them and allow intermediate catches.
The Giants’ WR1 has played a big role in the last two games, and it boggles the mind to think there could be more.
One part of this offense that is crying for attention is the ability this big rookie brings to the field. All he does is catch everything thrown his way, much like Likely catches everything in sight.
Fields didn’t get his first target until early in the third quarter, when he made a defender miss and took it for 13 yards, gaining five after contact and setting up a 3rd-and-2.
On the fourth-quarter game-tying drive, Fields took a 7-yard catch past the marker for a huge first down. These were his only two targets on the day.
His efficiency is off the charts. Since he’s on the field so much for his blocking, you would think the coaches and his quarterback might start looking his way a bit more.
As for his blocking, Fields needs to be more aware of the heavy pressure opposing corners put on the Giants’ running game and get a piece of his man, since those edge defenders are really in attack mode out there.

A third catch came on a gadget play from McCarthy, an actual 5-yard loss, but Mooney was poked in the face on the play and had to leave the game for a handful of plays.
He did drop a pass on a subsequent broken play, with the ball behind him in the wet conditions. Mooney returned after leaving and finished the game.
It felt like Likely caught about 20 balls out there, but his actual numbers were 11 receptions for 94 yards and two scores. After struggling to get in tune with Winston, this week was the first game in which the two looked in sync.
Once again, he didn’t drop a single pass, even though Likely had his fair share of lunging and low pass targets to execute in the pouring rain. He truly does have amazing hands.

title: Four Plays That Defined the Giants’ Wild 27-27 Tie With the Commanders
full_text:
The New York Giants and Washington Commanders played to a 27-27 tie in their first division meeting of the season, a wild game that ended with a result neither side wanted.
The Giants were lucky to be in position to win after Washington took control in the first half and looked like it would keep dominating.
New York staged a major comeback in the final two quarters behind an improved passing performance from Jameis Winston, who completed 33 of 54 pass attempts for 326 yards and three touchdowns to force overtime.
After an extra 10 minutes, neither team made enough plays to leave as the victor. Still, these four plays were the most impactful in leading both the Giants and Commanders to a strange finish.
The last two weeks of the Giants' slate brought plenty of praise for a defense that thwarted two consecutive final opposing drives to seal gritty wins over the Titans and Cardinals.
That same physicality didn't show up when the Commanders took the opening possession of Week 5. Washington came out looking to create chunk plays and found several against the Giants' unprepared unit.
It started with Rachaad White's 27-yard kickoff return, which set the Commanders up at their own 31-yard line. Three plays later, Jayden Daniels connected with tight end Chig Okonkwo for a 23-yard gain to enter New York territory in just over a minute.
On the next play, the Commanders caught the Giants defense sleeping again, scoring on a huge 33-yard run by running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt that finished in the end zone and gave the home team a fast 6-0 advantage, the extra point attempt being no good.
The drive took four plays and 69 yards, putting the Giants in a hole in exactly two minutes. It also marked the second straight week an opponent scored on its first possession against New York (the Cardinals scored an opening touchdown in eight  plays and 58 yards in Week 4).
The score immediately put the heat on Winston and the Giants offense to play catch-up in a game where throwing the ball in the rainy weather wasn't ideal.
The Giants got arguably their best effort from the receiving corps this season, and none of it would have been possible without Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely.
While the duo combined for 22 receptions, 215 yards, and three touchdowns, Likely's stat line (11 catches, 94 yards, 2 TDs) mattered more on the scoreboard. In particular, the tight end's second score nearly didn't happen.
On the Giants' second drive of the third quarter, Likely first found pay dirt on a three-yard connection from Winston, capping the team's longest drive of the game (13 plays, 63 yards). It also answered a 38-yard touchdown scramble by Daniels on the preceding Commanders possession that had grown Washington's lead to 19-6.
The Commanders dealt another blow to the comeback effort when Daniels broke free for a 26-yard keeper that found the end zone, and after Washington converted the two-point try, it was back ahead by two scores.
Once again, it was Likely who wouldn't say die on New York's fourth-quarter attempt to rally. No. 9 put his hands all over the Giants' next possession, catching a 10-yard pass to open the drive, then finishing it with a 16-yard catch-and-run that saw the ball come loose near the goal line.
After an officiating review, Likely had the wherewithal to extend the nose of the football over the plane of the end zone before Rasul Douglas punched it loose, nullifying the turnover and cementing his second touchdown, which pulled the Giants within a 27-20 deficit.
Had the ball really been coughed up, it might have been the lasting gut punch that took the wind out of the Giants' comeback sails.
Instead, Likely notched his third and fourth touchdowns of the year, his second game with multiple scores, and reminded everyone why the Giants made sure the rising star followed John Harbaugh from Baltimore to be a key weapon in their offense.
Though the Giants didn't lose, the tie was never more frustrating than in the final 3:38 of overtime, when they finally had the field position to attempt a game-winning field goal with Dominic Zvada and put the Commanders to bed.
After Zvada's earlier miss, the Giants defense had to come out with heavy pressure to force Daniels into mistakes and stall any movement toward field-goal range for Stevens.
It worked perfectly, as defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson's group got the Commanders offense off the field in four plays and 13 yards behind a forced fumble Washington recovered and a failed fourth-down conversion attempt that drew a delay-of-game penalty when the Giants couldn't be fooled into going offside.
The biggest stop of the afternoon put the ball back in the Giants' hands with a chance to steal the road win and improve to 4-1, but not before Big Blue's offense offered one more turnover to its count of two.
In eight plays and 67 yards, Winston led the Giants offense with two big completions to Nabers for 36 yards. Skattebo handled the rest of the work on the ground, punishing the Commanders' defense with a 19-yard burst followed by two more carries for a total of 14 yards.
With the Giants at the Washington 24-yard line and in Zvada's range, they tried one more carry to set up the next play, but Skattebo lost control of the ball, and the Commanders recovered it to stall the upset.
The crushing fumble wouldn't be the Giants' death knell, as the Commanders would one-up the mistake with an unfathomable case of time mismanagement that ripped away their own shot at a game-winning Stevens kick in the final seconds of the extra period.
For Skattebo and company, it was a play they'll be thinking about beyond Sunday. There had to be some trepidation given Zvada's shaky outing, but there was no better time to trust their young kicker to convert the one kick that would have wiped away the thought of his earlier misses.
Plus, the Giants' ball control has been an issue. Skattebo's mishap was the team's fifth fumble this season and the third they lost, both marks leading the NFL through five games.
One could also wonder what Harbaugh and the coaches were thinking when they elected to push for a few extra yards instead of shutting the door on the Commanders and leaving with a 2-0 record in the NFC East standings.
A tie is not a loss, but with one foolish handoff, the Giants cost themselves a little extra breathing room from their divisional neighbors.
Facing second-and-8 from the 24-yard line, well within field-goal range, the Commanders had no timeouts left and ran a play with no discernible purpose that ended with Daniels getting sacked.
Maybe they were trying to gain a few yards for a closer game-winning field goal. Maybe they wanted to burn time off the clock so that a miss wouldn't leave the Giants time to drive for a field goal attempt of their own.
Or maybe those involved forgot they had no timeouts. Whatever the reason, it was one of the more bizarre endings to a game, and a big reason the contest finished in a draw that increased the Giants' lead in the NFC East to 1.5 games.

title: Jameis Winston Answers Critics With Historic Day in Giants Tie vs. Commanders
full_text:
The adage that says “the backup quarterback is the most popular player on a football roster” is certainly alive and well, at least for the New York Giants .
Such has been the case ever since the Giants acquired J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings for a fifth-round pick.
For many pundits, the arrival of McCarthy, who took five snaps against the Commanders in a package of plays the coaches felt comfortable having him run, meant it was just a matter of time before Jameis Winston’s run as the starter, which has been frustrating at times, would come to an end.
Instead, Winston, who has joked about the “Jameis Winston Experience,” has handled his situation with aplomb and quieted some of those critics calling for McCarthy to take over at quarterback.
The part of the Jameis Winston experience that no one outside of the building sees is that he comes to work, puts in the effort, and is always open to getting better. While his weekly showings are not perfect—whose effort is?—he gives his teammates every chance possible for a win.
A wacky game against the Commanders ended in a 27-27 tie after a major collective brain freeze in overtime, when it appeared Washington forgot it had no timeouts left while driving for the game-winning score. Winston gave the Giants a chance.
The 12-year veteran led the team back from a 14-point deficit, completing 33 of 54 passes for 326 yards and three touchdowns for a passer rating of 96.7, and adding five carries for 27 yards.
It marked the only time since 1950 that a Giant has thrown for at least 300 yards and three touchdowns while rushing for at least 25 yards in the same game.
He also became the first Giants quarterback since Eli Manning on Sept. 24, 2017, to throw three or more touchdowns in the second half.
His passing efficiency, which started slow, improved as the game went on , thanks in part to a coaching adjustment to move away from the no-huddle, control the tempo, and return to the drop-back game.
Winston saved his best performance for the second half, going from 43.8% completion in the first 30 minutes to 75% in the second half, before capping it with a 50% completion rate in overtime.
“I thought he was amazing in the second half,” head coach John Harbaugh said of Winston.
“First half, he wasn’t. He’d be the first to tell you that, but that’s on everybody. I tell the guys, nothing good is all one person. We’re all responsible for all the good, and we’re all responsible for all the bad.”
Winston, who makes no secret of how much he leans into his faith, has surely heard the growing chatter about his current hold on the starting quarterback job and how McCarthy, whose skill set is thought to be closer to Jaxson Dart’s because of his mobility, should be handed the keys to the offense.
But Winston, as he did under pressure against Washington, plays his game.
“I always focus on what my heart desires, and I say this over and over again, I desire to be the New York Football Giants Super Bowl-winning quarterback,” he said.
“I desire to be a great starting quarterback in the NFL. I dreamed of this, and this is who I am, and I know that I’m going to continue to get better and find ways to help this team win football games.”
