title: Eagles Report Card: Grading Every Position Group and Head Coach After Five Games
full_text:
The Philadelphia Eagles have lost three in a row and, at 2-3, are under .500 for the first time in five years. The grades won’t look pretty on the team’s report card, and perhaps a litany of injuries is the reason.
Still, the offense has been dreadful in the second half. It's averaging 4.6 points, 97.4 total yards, and has 5 three-and-outs. All three stats are last in the NFL.
Here grades for each position and the head coach:
After looking like an MVP in the first two games, leading a game-winning touchdown drive that ended in a touchdown pass with just nine seconds left against the Titans, Jalen Hurts’ play has dropped. He hasn’t taken to Sean Mannion’s overhaul of the offense as quickly as one would have hoped, and he doesn’t always seem to see the entire field. His rebuilt offensive line could be part of that, but his decision-making hasn’t been where it needs to be, and his completion rate is a career-low 57.8 percent.
His ability to pick up yards with his legs has been neutralized, rushing only 23 times – most of that on scrambles from the pocket – 101 yards and one TD.
Still, he gets credit for his eight touchdowns to just three interceptions, as well as the job he did in the first two wins.
Saquon Barkley has been hurt early in two games and missed one already. At 29, can he rebound and still help this team when he gets healthy?
Meanwhile, Tank Bigsby is on injured reserve, and Will Shipley could be put on IR too, after E SPN’s Adam Schefter reported that Shipley suffered a partial tear of his plantar fascia during Sunday’s loss to the Jaguars and could miss multiple weeks. That leaves practice squad players Dameon Pierce and Carson Steele to carry the load.
The grade goes up from a ‘C’ because of Darius Cooper , who has four touchdowns on just seven catches. The Eagles haven't had a receiver since Jeremy Maclin in 2014 catch four touchdowns in the first five games of a season.
Tay Wicks has been decent, but the Rams’ Trent McDuffie took him out of the game in a Week 4 loss, and DeVonta Smith has missed two games with an injury. Makai Lemon has done some decent things and should only continue to get better and more involved.
Dallas Goedert picked up where he left off last year, snaring two touchdowns against the Commanders in the opener. Then he got hurt in Week 2 and missed two games. Johnny Mundt and E.J. Jenkins don’t provide much offense, and rookie Eli Stowers is on injured reserve. The Eagles signed Zach Ertz, but an impactful role for the veteran has yet to develop.
Lane Johnson retired, and Cam Jurgens was traded the very next day. The Eagles have had three different starting centers in just five games. Continuity is a big key to successful offensive line play, and there just hasn’t been any yet.
Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter were given big raises, but Davis isn’t having the same impact he did last year. He played 61 percent of the snaps a season ago, but is playing just 46 percent this year.
Carter, on the other hand, has been playing with a broken bone in his wrist, which has hampered him, but his three sacks lead the team, and his five tackles for loss equal the number of TFLs he had last year.
Jalyx Hunt looked like a double-digit sack artist in the making, but he has none. Nolan Smith has two sacks, but he hasn’t shown the play-in, play-out consistency he should have at this point in his career. The big offseason acquisition, Jonathan Greenard, has missed three games with two different injuries and has played just 37 snaps. As for free agents Arnold Ebiketie and A.J. Epenesa, they haven’t contributed much so far.
Zack Baun continues to play at a high level, though he missed a game due to a concussion, which was the first time he missed a game with an injury since arriving here in 2024. Jeremiah Trotter Jr. was a force in his only start, collecting 15 tackles, and could be taking over the starting job from Jihaad Campbell, last year's first-round pick, who has been up and down.
Quinyon Mitchell notched his first regular-season interception in Week 5, adding to the four he has in the postseason. But neither he nor Cooper DeJean seems to be playing at the level they played at last year, when they both earned All-Pro honors, and Riq Woolen hasn’t had the bounce-back season the Eagles hoped he would have.
One of the team’s biggest question marks entering the season was here. It is more a liability than a question mark at this point. Andrew Mukuba remains inconsistent. Marcus Epps is hurt, but he wasn’t turning heads in the first three games he played before getting banged up. Michael Carter has done some decent things at the position, but the Eagles severely limited here.
The one and only ‘A’ on this report card is well deserved, with Jake Elliott already connecting on both tries beyond 50 yards, Braden Mann looking like an All-Pro, and Rocco Underwood flawless with his long snaps.
When your head coach has to admit to costing the team a game , as Nick Sirianni did after the loss in London, that’s not good. Neither is being 2-3.

title: Nick Sirianni's 'Flower' Speech as Relevant as Ever for Eagles in 2026
full_text:
Another two weeks and it might be time for the speech: “We talkin’ 'bout PRACTICE?”
This one: “It’s really important that the foundation is being built and the roots are going out and the only way the roots are growing, and they get stronger and they grow better is that we all water, we all fertilize so that when it pops out, it really pops out. … keep watering and look at yourself. Are you fertilizing every day? So, when it’s time to pop, it’ll pop.”
That was Nick Sirianni on Oct. 27, 2021. He showed his team a flower during a team meeting and gave that speech. It was his first season as a head coach, and his team had lost four in a row to drop to 2-5. He was on the hot seat. He always seems to be, but back then, seven games in, it was a seat glowing red.
That fiery glow is back. The Eagles have lost three in a row and, at 2-3, are below .500 for the first time since, yep, Sirianni’s first season in town.
My assertion has always been that Sirianni’s strength as a coach is building a culture in the locker room. He does it by insisting on connections between players and coaches, because when adversity strikes, they have only each other to lean on.
Too many think he wins because of the talent given to him. What successful coach doesn’t win with talent general managers give them? The difference is not all of them win the ultimate prize. Sirianni bridges that difference.
In the “water and fertilizer” speech, he talked about always having a different message to give to the team. Fast forward to today, and if they ever need to hear another Sirianni message, it’s right now.
Will this team prove that it is committed to each other? Will they stay together as one and not splinter? It's that kind of week.
“This is where relationships come into play,” said Sirianni on the day after his team lost a heartbreaker, 19-17, in London. “You're constantly communicating with the guys through messages with the team in a team setting but also checking in with guys on as much as you possibly can throughout the week.”
Sirianni was sold to the fan base upon his hire as an offensive-minded coach. That was until he turned playcalling duties over to Shane Steichen after that 2-5 start. That is another Sirianni strength: the ability to make a move when one needs to be made. The way he did not just with Steichen but also when he fired defensive coordinator Sean Desai midway through the 2023 season and replaced him with Matt Patricia.
Steichen worked; Patricia did not. Not all his moves pay off. The point is he isn’t afraid to change things when needed.
His speech on that October day five years ago led to some eye rolls, furrowed brows, quizzical looks, and set the airwaves ablaze: “He’s overmatched.”
Who knew then that the Eagles would become one of the most beautiful flowers fans had probably seen in their lifetimes?
After that speech, they went 7-3 and made the playoffs.
After that speech, the Eagles have done nothing but post double-digit winning seasons, win three NFC East championships, including back-to-back crowns to break a string of 21 consecutive seasons without a repeat winner of the division.
After that speech, they went to two Super Bowls, winning one, and it could have very easily been two if not for some heavy-handed officiating late in the game that virtually ensured the Chiefs the title that year.
“Right now, we are what our record says we are,” said Sirianni. “We're 2-3. We know there's a lot left in the season, and I don't think that there is any panic on any aspect of any player or coach in this building. We've had three-game losing streaks before. Our job is to get up and keep fighting.”

title: McMullen: Eagles’ Second-Half Offense Has Become a Vanishing Act
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA - Through five games, the Philadelphia Eagles sit at 2-3 after a third straight setback, a 19-17 gut-wrencher to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London sealed by Cam Little’s 57-yard field goal as time expired.
Nick Sirianni took the blame for the kickoff decision in the waning seconds that allowed the return that set up Little’s heroics, and he also took accountability for losing the game.
However, the bigger and far more persistent problem was the offense’s disappearance after halftime – again.
In the second half of the last three games, the Eagles have produced: three points, 10 three-and-outs, 12 first downs, and a 2-for-20 mark on third down over 18 drives. League-wide, they rank last in  second-half scoring (23 points), total yards (495), three-and-out rate (51.7 percent), and pass yards per attempt (4.0).
Across the first five games, Sean Mannion’s new-look offense has repeatedly built or held first-half leads only to watch drives stall, punts pile up, and opportunities to close games evaporate.
Injuries have not helped—Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith were out in London, the offensive line has been reshuffled due to circumstance and injury, and the run game has been sporadic at best (just 22 yards against the Jaguars).
But the pattern predates the latest absences and echoes issues from last season under Kevin Patullo.
Mannion, who calls plays from the booth in a scheme supposedly influenced by Shanahan-McVay principles, has yet to produce consistent second-half rhythm, third-down efficacy, or explosive plays when the game tightens. It’s been a repetitive offense that has been easily solved by opponents.
Sirianni, speaking Monday, framed the response around collective growth rather than blame when asked about Mannion by Eagles On SI.
“I think that right now, offensively, we all have to be better… players, coaches with myself - all of us have to be better,” the head coach admitted. “We’re not worried about gauging where this person is or where that person is. We’re worried about growth… Obviously it hasn’t been good enough.”
“It’s never just one thing,” Sirianni continued. “… We all have things that we have to get better at… We won’t ever use anything as an excuse… It’s about finding solutions.”
There was an obvious disconnect with Sirianni noting “you have to be different to give yourself an edge” in the NFL, an interesting take as so many teams around the league are playing a similar style of offense, and the Eagles are late to that party.
“You have to take accountability and not look to assign blame, and look yourself in the mirror first,” said Sirianni. “… To do things in the NFL and to win games in the NFL, you have to be different.”
The Eagles offense ranks near the bottom of the league in points and yards per game overall; the under-center and play-action elements have not clicked at the expected rate, and third-down and second-half stalls have become the only real consistency.
Another high-expectations team facing a similar early-season offensive stall has already acted more decisively.
In Denver, Sean Payton reclaimed play-calling duties from first-year offensive coordinator Davis Webb after just four games. The Broncos were 2-2 and ranked near the bottom of the league in scoring and total yards (around 27th in both) when Payton announced the change after a loss to the 49ers, saying simply, “We’ll make a change offensively. I’ll call the plays.”
Webb remains the coordinator and is involved in game-planning, but Payton is now the voice in Bo Nix’s ear.
Both situations involve a veteran head coach who previously called plays, handing the role to a young, first-time play-caller amid high expectations, only to watch the offense sputter with too many three-and-outs, limited explosiveness, and an inability to sustain drives.
The difference is the timeline and the response: Payton judged four games a sufficient sample and stepped back in; Sirianni continues to emphasize growth, shared accountability, and incremental improvement, with Mannion still calling the plays.
Sirianni also doesn’t want to take play-calling back, but has former Tampa Bay OC Josh Grizzard on staff as the passing game coordinator as a potential contingency option.
Whether the Eagles’ more tempered approach yields the growth Sirianni craves or whether the second-half disappearing act continues and forces a Sean Desai-like bolder adjustment will define the season.
The idea that the Eagles should punt on the campaign is shortsighted given how poor the NFC East is shaping up. Winning the division is an easy path to a sixth straight postseason berth and the kind of sustained success that has been Philadelphia’s seasonal goal since Andy Reid brought the philosophy to the organization in 1999.
Maybe the Super Bowl isn’t realistic this season, but dismissing playoff experience as not good enough for the younger players is specious.
The defense is getting better. The offense, particularly after intermission, has not. As Sirianni put it, the job now is to find solutions. In an industry defined by results, gauging Mannion's job performance is inevitable. If the head coach refuses, someone else will.
The window for growth is narrowing, and Payton's urgency exhibited in Denver may be the template for changing the voice on the headset unless Mannion figures this out.

title: McMullen: Nick Sirianni's 'Accountability' Claim Rings Hollow as Situational Failures Mount
full_text:
To know Nick Sirianni is to understand the Eagles coach’s obsession with situational football.
For that reason, Sunday’s late-game implosion in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars was the exact kind of failure Sirianni cannot afford.
In a matter of moments, Jake Elliott’s 48-yard field goal had the heavily slanted Eagles crowd in a celebratory mood, with the pubs surrounding Tottenham Hotspur Stadium preparing for the onslaught of midnight green.
To those who value results over process, Cam Little’s 57-yard bomb seven seconds later that resulted in a 19-17 Jags win meant the most sensible decision with Jacksonville out of timeouts was instructing Elliott to try for a touchback on the subsequent kickoff after his successful boot, or at least a more controlled “dirty kick” to make things tougher on veteran kick returner Ameer Abdullah.
Instead, Elliott aimed a typical kickoff directly into the landing zone, and Abdullah returned it 53 yards to the Eagles’ 39-yard line.
Had Philadelphia’s kickoff coverage executed none of this, it would not even be thought about, or never mind, discussed. There's a lot to that, though, starting with the fact that one of the Eagles' top coverage players -- Jeremiah Trotter Jr. -- was ejected for scuffling on the opening kickoff that was returned for a touchdown by Jags rookie Josh Cameron before being wiped out by offsetting penalties.
On the final kickoff, after taking the lead and needing to circumvent only eight seconds, Arnold Ebiketie was a little loose with his lane discipline, and Abdullah burst through the gap. Ultimately, fate took over from there when Jonathan Jones caught the speedy running back, but he did it one second too soon.
To the torch and pitchfork crowd, all that was validated was that Sirianni’s miscue was the reason a trip to the United Kingdom felt empty and the coach wasn’t in the mood to put up any kind of fight afterward.
“What hurts there is that the guys fought so hard and then I don’t make the decision that I should make at the end of the game and I cost us that game,” said Sirianni.
He told the locker room the same thing, taking the kind of accountability that will resonate in-house. That’s also the right public stance, even if it does not erase the damage.
As a CEO coach, though, situational football is the area Sirianni has long presented as a strength. He drills it relentlessly beyond the obvious third-down and two-minute spots.
Sirianni talks process until the word almost loses meaning. He wants his teams to take pride in winning by any way that is required. Saturdays are spent going over every possible game-day scenario.
Late-game special teams strategy and clock management sit squarely in that lane, as does Makai Lemon stepping out of bounds instead of forcing Jacksonville to take its third and final timeout, two plays before Elliott stepped on the field to kick his FG.
Had Lemon gone down before crossing the sideline, the Eagles would have bled the clock to three seconds, and Elliott’s kick would have been the game-winner.
Sirianni’s public accountability comes across as empty when he fails to explain the fallout.
“If I followed it, the process, then obviously that turns out to be the wrong decision,” he said. “If I didn’t follow it, then obviously that was the wrong decision.
“Either way, I’m wrong. That’s all I’ll say about that.”
A coach who treats process as the North Star cannot land on “either way, I’m wrong” without the foundation looking cracked.
Owning the result while declining to explain the reasoning leaves the process looking more like a plot twist than a working tool.
That’s not acceptable for a CEO coach.

title: Eagles-Jaguars Stock Report: Nick Sirianni Takes Accountability for Late-Game Collapse
full_text:
The Philadelphia Eagles suffered a disappointing 19-17 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday in London, dropping their third straight game in a dramatic finish at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.
Philadelphia, missing Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith while dealing with a patchwork offensive line, built a 14-7 halftime lead on a Will Shipley two-yard touchdown run and a 62-yard catch-and-run score from Jalen Hurts to Darius Cooper.
The offense then stalled completely after the break, managing just three second-half points, while rushing for a dismal 2 yards on 18 carries and finishing with 232 total yards against Jacksonville’s 408-yard output.
Trevor Lawrence threw for 331 yards and two touchdowns (both to Parker Washington), including a 27-yard fourth-down score that put the Jaguars ahead 16-14 late in the game. Cam Little missed the ensuing extra point, thanks to a backup long snapper, allowing Jake Elliott’s 48-yard field goal with eight seconds remaining to give the Eagles a 17-16 lead.
However, Ameer Abdullah returned the kickoff 53 yards to the Philadelphia 38-yard line, setting up Little’s game-winning 57-yard field goal as time expired. Nick Sirianni took the accountability afterward, saying he “lost us that game."
The Game-Wrecker: Jalen Carter set the tone with a first half for the ages against a pedestrian Jacksonville interior offensive line. The gifted Eagles' defensive tackle has two sacks, two forced fumbles, three tackles for loss, five pressures, and three run stops.
That's an NFC Defensive Player of the Month performance in 30 minutes of football and a signal that the Jaguars were in for a fight despite the game being dubbed an early Super Bowl contender vs. an injury-depleted mess.
Third-down life: The Eagles entered the contest having failed on their last 17 third-down attempts, dating back to Week 3 vs. Chicago. On Sunday in London, they converted their first third-down when Jalen Hurts found Dallas Goedert for a 5-yard gain on a third-and-three play.
Goedert missed the past two games with an MCL injury, and his presence was comforting for Hurts, who trusts the veteran tight end. Overall, Philadelphia finished 6-for-15 on third down. They also started 4-for-6 before finishing 2-for-9, so it's not all peaches and cream, but an incremental improvement.
Young o-linemen: The thought of center Jake Majors and left guard Willie Lampkin making their first NFL starts, and right tackle Markel Bell making his second start, was projected as too much to overcome.
However, all three took their opportunities and battled. It wasn't always pretty, but the trio played well enough for the Eagles' offense to operate in a similar fashion to what it usually does. The play was good enough to win, as evidenced by holding the lead with eight seconds remaining.
Missed Opportunity: After playing well in Week 4 as a replacement for All-Pro Zack Baun, who could not get through the concussion protocol, Jeremiah Trotter Jr. was set to start again. With Baun back, Trotter was going to start for the struggling Jihaad Campbell, who missed some practice time with a knee issue.
However, Trotter was tossed from the game on the opening kickoff, as he and linebacker Bryan Thomas Jr. were ejected for scuffling. It was way too heavy-handed by the officials, but Trotter can't put himself in that position. Campbell ended up playing the whole game next to Baun, indicating that his potential benching wasn't fully injury-related.
.500: The Eagles fell to 2-3 with Sunday's loss, making it the first time since 2021 that the franchise has been underwater during the regular season. Philadelphia isn't used to being in this position, which will make Howie Roseman's approach at the trade deadline even more interesting.
More injuries: You can add to the Eagles' injury list with two more notable contributors: Will Shipley and edge defender Jalyx Hunt.
Shipley, who was starting because Barkley and Tank Bigsby were both out, left with a foot injury in the second quarter and didn't return.
Hunt went down on the last play of the first half with what was described as an ankle and knee issue. After the game, he was seen by reporters in a walking boot, and the early concern is a high ankle sprain and an MCL issue, according to an NFL source. If that's the case, Hunt will be out for multiple weeks.
Kickoff coverage/end of game management: The kickoff coverage looked leaky from the opening kick, which was taken to the house by the Jaguars and wiped out by multiple penalties.
With eight seconds remaining after Elliott kicked a 48-yard field goal to seemingly steal the game, Philly kicked it to Ameer Abdullah, instead of playing it safe with a touchback. He returned it 53 yards and gave Little an opportunity from 57. Even with a backup long snapper who was wild high all day, the strong-legged Little was true.
It's also fair to highlight the two plays before Elliott's FG: an incompletion and a completion to Makai Lemon, where the rookie receiver went out of bounds. The Eagles' failure to force the Jags to use their final timeout there enabled them to use it to secure the eight seconds Abdullah and Little needed to play the heroes.
The travel narrative: The Eagles left South Philadelphia late Friday at 10:45 p.m. ET. The idea was to get to London, which is about a seven-hour flight and five hours ahead of the East Coast, in the middle of the day, power through Saturday, and keep the body clocks as normal as possible. The plan was developed with the understanding that the Eagles have to come back next week and host Carolina on Sunday, so it was essentially a two-week plan. None of it impacted the game, despite many trying to shoehorn it as a potential issue before kickoff.

title: Nick Sirianni Owns Up to Poor, Late-Game Decision Making in Loss to Jaguars
full_text:
Nick Sirianni blew it. He knew it, too, and admitted it.
“I didn't make the right decision, and I lost us that game,” said the Eagles coach after his team lost for a third straight time, this time to the Jacksonville Jaguars, 19-17, in Week 5. “...The guys fought so hard, and then I didn't make the decision that I should have made at the end of the game, and I cost us that game, and I put that fully on me.”
He could have owned up to a pair of mistakes in the game’s dying seconds.
First, his decision not to let Jake Elliott kick the ball into the end zone after Elliott’s 48-yard field goal gave the Eagles a 17-16 lead with eight seconds left in the game. With no timeouts, the Jags would have needed one play to get into field goal range.
Ameer Abdullah took the short kick gift and raced 52 yards, allowing for one more play: a 57-yard field goal attempt by Cam Little, which he made as time expired.
Second, for his decision not to drain more of the game clock after the Eagles’ offense somehow showed a spark of life and made a first down at the Jaguars’ 34 with 25 seconds left, trailing 16-14.
The Eagles were already in Elliott’s field-goal range at that point. He's been hot so far this season, making two 50-plus-yard kicks in two attempts. Instead of running the ball once or twice, two passes were dialed up. The first was incomplete, stopping the clock. The second went to Makai Lemon, who ran an out pattern and got out of bounds after picking up seven yards, again stopping the clock.
Finally, the Eagles ran the ball. The play lost three yards, and the Jaguars called their final timeout, something they might have done if the Eagles had run on first or second down. That would have meant the Eagles could have run their field goal unit out to attempt the kick as the clock wound down to under five seconds. By not doing that, there was still time on the clock to do what Jacksonville did.
“I'm prepared as a quarterback to not worry about those things,” quarterback Jalen Hurts told reporters when asked if he would have done anything differently in those final 25 seconds. “I'm honoring the play call, honoring the things that are coming in the game. When I'm up at night, yeah, I think about them. Should I have said something or should I have took a step back and said, ‘Wait?’ Ultimately, there's a commitment to that and going out there and executing. And this was one where it did not work in our favor.”
But the decision not to kick off into the end zone was coaching negligence. There’s a time and place to trust your tacklers on kickoff coverage, but this wasn’t the time or place.
The Jags opened the game with a kickoff return for a touchdown, but it was called back on a holding penalty. Additionally, t he Eagles were without more than half a dozen injured players , including one of their top special teams tacklers, Jeremiah Trotter Jr. , who was ejected on the opening kickoff.
The players charged with tackling Abdullah, Kelee Ringo, Jonathan Jones, and Arnold Ebiketie had no chance.
“It sucks,” Elliott told reporters after the heartbreaking loss. “I mean, you come all this way, you think you're in the driver's seat to win a big game and now we're feeling pretty down.”
So, Sirianni stood before the players in the postgame locker room and let them know this loss was on him.
“I think it's so important for every person to take accountability, because that's the only way you get better,” said the coach. “You build trust that way. … just sick the way that went, and my decision went there."
These two decisions could haunt the Eagles for the remainder of the season and could ultimately lead to Sirianni getting fired if the season doesn’t end with a playoff game.

title: 5 Winners, 5 Losers, & More From Eagles' Heartbreaking 19-17 Loss to the Jaguars
full_text:
The Philadelphia Eagles’ special teams won it. Then lost it.
Jake Elliott kicked a 48-yard field goal with eight seconds left, but a breakdown in the Eagles special teams’ kickoff coverage led to a 57-yard game-winner from Cam Little as time expired, giving the Jacksonville Jaguars a 19-17 Week 5 win in London .
Say what you want about all the injuries the Eagles have endured this season, but it's been their offense’s inability to do anything – nothing, really - in the second half that has led to this losing streak. The Eagles have scored just three second-half points in the last three games. The three they got from Elliott looked like they would win the game, but it wasn't to be.
The Eagles barely get first downs over the final two quarters. That ineptitude has left their defense hung out to dry and gassed when the fourth quarter arrives.
The loss dropped the Eagles to 2-3. It is the first time they are below .500 since 2021, which was Nick Sirianni’s first year as the head coach. It’s an amazing stat, as is the team’s second-half scoring drought.
The Eagles’ outing wasn’t without effort, especially in the first half as they forged a 14-7 lead, scoring two touchdowns, which were the first two first-half TDs the Jaguars allowed all season.
The Eagles, who didn't have superstars DeVonta Smith and Saquon Barkley, will host the Panthers next Sunday and entertain the Cowboys on Monday Night Football in Week 7.
Let’s get to some winners and losers:
Jalen Carter: The defensive tackle had an NFC East Defensive Player of the Week performance. He dominated in the first half, sacking Trevor Lawrence twice and forcing a fumble on both, though the Jaguars recovered both. He had four tackles, including three for loss.
Darius Cooper: Last year’s undrafted free agent ran a great route to get wide open, and Jalen Hurts hit him in stride for a 62-yard touchdown, giving the Eagles a 14-7 lead with 5:36 to play in the second quarter, which was the difference at halftime. He now has four touchdowns on the season .
DARIUS COOPER 62 YARDS!!! pic.twitter.com/TTJayV78mF
Willie Lampkin: The shortest player to start on the offensive line in an NFL game in a long, long time, the 5-foot-11 left guard paved the way on Will Shipley’s two-yard touchdown run to tie the score in the first quarter.
Quinyon Mitchell: The Eagles' defense made two defensive stands, and the cornerback was involved in both. The first was at the goal line, when he broke up a third-down throw in the end zone on a pass from the 1-yard line in the dying seconds of the first half.
Mitchell also recorded his first career regular-season pick later in the game. However, a failed fourth-down conversion by the Eagles' offense gave the Jags good field position late in the third quarter.
Eagles fans: Very few fan bases travel as well as Philly’s. They took over Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, booing the Jaguars, who aren’t used to that because they were the home team and play in London every year. It sounded and looked like a home game at Lincoln Financial Field.
Special teams: There's no way you can give up a 52-yard kickoff return to Ameer Abdullah with eight seconds left, putting the Jaguars in position to win, but Michael Clay’s kickoff return team did just that. Why not kick the ball into the end zone? With no timeouts and eight seconds left, the Jaguars would have had to do something heroic to get into field position.
Sean Mannion: He’s the offensive coordinator, so he has to bear the brunt of the miserable failures of the second half. With an offensive line in disarray and starting young players, why not use Carson Steele as a fullback, giving the offense an extra blocker in the run game? The Eagles ran for a minuscule 22 yards.
Jonathan Greenard: The outside linebacker missed five games last year with a shoulder injury that required surgery. He already had a pec strain and now has an ankle injury. After much pregame discussion, it was determined Greenard couldn’t play. His loss was particularly glaring when Jalyx Hunt needed help to get off the field with an injury on the last play of the first half.
Greenard has played 37 snaps so far this season. The Eagles made a big investment in him , signing him to a four-year extension for nearly $100 million, which hasn’t paid dividends -- yet.
Andrew Mukuba: Vic Fangio keeps saying he is happy with how the second-year safety has been playing, but sometimes his play speaks otherwise. For example, Mukuba was beaten badly on a short throw to Parker Washington, a sixth-round pick out of Penn State three years ago, which led to a 51-yard touchdown for Jacksonville.
Parker Washington just keeps making plays. @PHIvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/swaHaZV4sI
Jeremiah Trotter Jr.'s ejection: This goes to the official. Trotter appeared to be pancaking Bryan Thomas Jr. on the opening kickoff, then Thomas used both legs to kick Trotter as he rolled to the ground. Not sure how either player was ejected, but it was a big loss for the Eagles, who were set to start Trotter ahead of Jihaad Campbell.

title: Eagles' Dameon Pierce Has a Strong Benefactor in Nick Sirianni
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA — Dameon Pierce has arrived on the Eagles’ 53-man roster and could be a major contributor during Sunday’s game in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
The veteran running back has a strong benefactor in Philadelphia head coach Nick Sirianni.
The Eagles promoted the former Houston Texan off their practice squad this week. The move comes as injury thins the backfield—Saquon Barkley was ruled out Friday with a hamstring issue and backup Tank Bigsby is on injured reserve with a core muscle injury—leaving Pierce and Will Shipley as the healthy options behind an offense that needs production on the ground.
Asked what steered him back to Philadelphia after he was a victim on the initial cut to 53, Pierce did not hesitate. “ Nick Sirianni, ” he said, laughing, before explaining why.
“He’s a great guy. He’s vibrant. He loves the game of football. He loves what he does. And this locker room, to gel, we all gotta have good relationships,” Pierce said.
Sirianni returned the sentiment of Friday when asked about his relationship with Pierce by Eagles On SI.
The coach said the Eagles had tracked Pierce since he came out of Florida.
“There’re a lot of guys [in the draft] you end up loving that it’s like, ‘Oh man, he’s going to be good for them,’” Sirianni said. “I think it all started back then, and just like I said, it’s fun being around him. He brings constant energy to the football team. He’s obviously a very talented player and works extremely hard and runs extremely hard."
“I’m excited for his opportunity.”
That opportunity has been a long time coming. Pierce burst onto the scene as a rookie in 2022, rushing for 939 yards and four touchdowns on 220 carries for the Texans while adding 30 receptions for 165 yards. He was one of the league’s more productive first-year backs.
What followed was a steep drop: 416 yards in 2023, a reduced role and injuries (including ankle, hamstring and shoulder issues) in the years after, and only 26 yards on 10 carries in four games in 2025 before Houston waived him.
Pierce said the years of limited snaps were navigated with prayer and mental toughness.
“Being in this game, you gotta have a lot of mental strength, on the field and off the field,” he said. “Just finding that happy medium to where you can go and just control what you can control and be ready when the time is, for sure has helped.”
Pierce described the recent promotion as everything he has been working toward.
“Just having a lot of the mental toughness I had over the last few years, you know, probably not going the way I wanted it, but I’m all about timing,” Pierce said. “Just making sure I’m prepared on that field, making sure I’m ready to carry the torch for my guy.”
For Eagles fans who have not seen much of him, Pierce offered a short self-portrait: a down-to-earth player from South Georgia with humble roots, who tries to be detailed and explosive.
“I just try to bring the game to the defense, not try to let them dictate my game speed. If it’s there, take it. If not, wait on it,” he said.
Whether that translates into early-down work against one of the league’s better run defenses remains to be seen.
What is clear is that Pierce has been preparing for his second chance and Sirianni is excited to provide it for him.

title: Bringing in Andy Dalton Was a Mistake, One Howie Roseman Admitted When He Cut Him
full_text:
Andy Dalton was a mistake. Right from the very start, trading a seventh-round pick for the veteran quarterback just seven months ago made little sense then and even less now after general manager Howie Roseman admitted to the error by cutting Dalton before he was able to get on a plane to London for Week 5.
Why it took so long, only Roseman knows. Why he did it in the first place, only he knows.
The Eagles already had a capable backup in Tanner McKee and you knew they were going to take one in the draft after the QB they took in the 2025 draft, Kyle McCord, fled to Green Bay and then was traded to the Miami, where he serves as the backup to Malik Willis on the still-winless Dolphins.
And Roseman did, selecting Cole Payton in the fifth round. But it gets weirder.
The Eagles allowed Dalton and McKee to battle to be the backup. McKee, who is in the final year of his contract, was a good soldier about the battle, noting that every year you have to compete for your job.
The question of who Jalen Hurts’ top backup would be was a topic all summer. Head coach Nick Sirianni allowed it to remain an issue—and a distraction to a point—by not naming the backup even after the 53-man roster was set. It wasn't until the morning of the season opener that there was any clarity on who would be the No. 2.
Even the decision to keep four quarterbacks on the 53-man-roster was strange, especially because they had to part ways with Cam Latu, Cameron Williams, and others who had a better chance of helping this team than Dalton.
But they didn’t want to cut Payton and try to get him to the practice squad because they were apparently afraid another team would poach him.
Dalton’s resume was longer than McKee's. He had played in 179 games, with 169 starts, over 15 years. The Eagles were his sixth team. He threw one pass in his short stint in Philly. A Bears rookie safety intercepted it in the end zone.
The Eagles drafted McKee. They knew more about him from being up close with him than Dalton. McKee was a sixth-round pick in 2023. He made two starts, going 1-1. He played in six games and threw five touchdowns to just one interception.
It was a strange thing to watch him have to fight for his job. The Eagles could have saved a seventh-round pick next year and not traded for Dalton.
Granted, neither looked good this summer, and now Payton is an injury to Hurts and another one to McKee from being a starter. The way this season has gone, with one injury after another to key players, would it surprise anyone if that scenario eventually plays out?
Still, it was the wrong move, and a weird one to bring in Dalton. At least Roseman admitted it, even if it took four weeks of the regular season for him to do it.

title: 3 Eagles Lineup Decisions I'd Make If I Was Nick Sirianni in Week 5
full_text:
Nick Sirianni and the Philadelphia Eagles are outgunned and outmanned walking into London for a Week 5 showdown against the Jacksonville Jaguars. They are without eight starters going into Sunday . That's over a third of the team's starting lineup from Week 1.
As the Eagles offense tries to put pieces together, Sirianni is under pressure to try and get things right across the board. Going into Week 5, though, the Eagles should make three roster moves ahead of kickoff.
Philadelphia hasn't gotten the kind of quality play at safety compared to the last several years. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio has said he doesn't want to move nickel corner Cooper DeJean to safety, but the Eagles do have a contingency plan in place to make that happen. Kenny Moore was one of the better cornerbacks in the slot for a very long time.
If he is up to the task, he could shift to nickel, and that would allow DeJean to roam around the defense and secure the backend of Philadelphia's secondary. There has been precedent as well. Kyle Hamilton is considered the best safety in the league but actually played in the slot for several years to try and help Baltimore's secondary.
DeJean isn't a natural safety, but his skill set and versatility could put him in that same boat.
Philadelphia is operating out of 11 personnel (or one tight end on the field) over 70% of the time this season. That needs to be even higher going forward. The Eagles are better at giving their offensive line space to operate in 11 personnel compared to the condensed look that comes with a second tight end on the field.
With so many backups now starting this season, Philadelphia needs to be able to run the ball effectively. Shortening the field has done nothing for them over the last few seasons.
They need to get their best players out in space. On Sunday, that's exactly how they can move the ball.
The jury is out. The Eagles have struggled mightily against the blitz all season far. A big part of that is due to the fact that the team has struggled with their offensive line's health for most of the start of the season.
The best remedy to any blitz is to get the ball out quickly. It's also something that the Eagles and Hurts have struggled to do over the last few years. In last week's loss to the Rams, Philadelphia saw several short throws batted at the line of scrimmage.
Against a Jaguars defense that is among the most opportunistic units in the league, the Eagles need Hurts to get the ball out quick and let their receivers start making plays after the catch.

title: Steelers Could Get Rico Dowdle Back at Perfect Time
full_text:
Pittsburgh Steelers running back Rico Dowdle appears to be on the precipice of a return from his toe injury.
While praising Jaylen Warren during his postgame press conference following the Steelers ' Week 5 win over the Indianapolis Colts, head coach Mike McCarthy stated that Dowdle was "close" to suiting up in the contest and that he's hopeful he'll make his return in Week 6 vs. the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
“He's the man. He's hauling it right now for us," McCarthy said. "There's a number you like to continue to give him. He's produced. So it's been heavy. It'll be great to get Rico back this week too. I'd love for Rico to practice this week and, hopefully, be up for the game. Yeah, he was close. Having him as a one-two punch was the vision of this offense, but Jaylen's crushing it right now. He's been awesome for us.”
Pittsburgh is in dire straits at the wide receiver position.
Michael Pittman Jr. was placed on the reserve/injured list after aggravating his foot injury last week, meaning he'll need to miss at least another three games. That period will run through the team's Week 9 bye, meaning the earliest he can return is in Week 10 vs. the Cincinnati Bengals.
Meanwhile, Roman Wilson (finger) and Ben Skowronek (calf) both went down in the first half against the Colts and did not play at all in the second half. That left DK Metcalf, Germie Bernard, Kaden Wetjen and Brandon Smith, who was elevated from the practice squad, as the only healthy receivers left on the game day roster.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler has reported that Wilson is expected to miss several weeks with his injury, though he is still in the process of gathering information and will seek out a second opinion.
As such, Pittsburgh is lacking depth at receiver and should have a move or two on the horizon to address that situation.
Obviously Dowdle isn't going to help mask the team's issues at the position in a traditional sense, but should he be back on the field against Tampa Bay, he does have the means to make a difference in the passing game.
The Steelers have often relied heavily on their running backs through the air. That was the case last season in Arthur Smith's system, as Kenneth Gainwell had 486 yards on 73 catches while Warren finished with 333 yards over 40 receptions, and the latter has now accumulated 230 receiving yards on 19 catches under Mike McCarthy this year.
Dowdle had posted four receptions for 28 yards in roughly a game-and-a-half before dislocating his toe twice in Week 2 against the Patriots, which has kept him out ever since.
The 28-year-old logged a combined 546 yards and four touchdowns across 78 catches between the 2024 and 2025 campaigns, though, showing that he is capable of making a real impact as a pass catcher out of the backfield and thus could be another key target for Rodgers as Pittsburgh deals with a shortage at receiver for the time being.
Coming into the season, the expectation was that Warren and Dowdle would share the workload at running back with something like a 55/45 or 60/40 split in favor of the former.
That was largely true when Dowdle was healthy, as he had 10 touches in Week 1 vs. the Atlanta Falcons while Warren had 15.
Given how dominant Warren has been since Dowdle went down, however, posting 491 yards from scrimmage in three games while looking like one of the league's top running backs, that type of split is unlikely to materialize moving forward.
Dowdle is a fantastic complementary piece at running back, though he's going to have to take a back seat to Warren.
Instead of a 1A, 1B-type situation, Warren has become the clear top dog for Pittsburgh and is in line to garner somewhere in the ballpark of 70 to 75 percent touches out of the backfield while Dowdle essentially gets the rest.
That could change at some point, but the Steelers simply can't curtail Warren's workload given how well he has played recently.

title: Steelers Make Right Call With Jaylen Warren
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Pittsburgh Steelers face a mountain of injuries after their Week 5 victory. Despite emerging with the win, the Steelers lost two key players, at least.
During his weekly press conference, head coach Mike McCarthy shared that wide receivers Roman Wilson and Ben Skowronek have already been ruled out for the team’s next contest against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
The Steelers will need to adjust their offensive game plan once again, but the one thing that won’t change is the reliance on running back Jaylen Warren. Asked about how he plans to utilize his backfield once Rico Dowdle returns from injury, McCarthy was clear that Warren is the key piece of the Steelers’ offensive puzzle.
”Jaylen’s our featured player right now. Let’s make sure we all recognize that. He’s hot. He’s playing great football for us,” McCarthy stated . “So it’s important for us as an offense, you know, coaches and players alike, to continue to put him in position to make plays. So, that won’t change.”
Dowdle is expected to return to the field this week after missing the last three games.
McCarthy’s comments are the biggest endorsement of Warren so far, and it comes at a time when he has become undeniable. Even if McCarthy had a different product envisioned for his backfield in the offseason, Warren has forced his hand for the better.
Since Dowdle’s injury, Warren has become the best piece of the offense by a wide margin. He’s received at least 15 carries in three straight contests, and he’s posted rushing yard totals of 127, 93 and 101 yards.
The question that gets asked based off of Warren’s history in the NFL, is, can the Steelers keep using him this frequently? Luckily for the offense, Warren is looking even healthier entering Week 6. McCarthy said that compared to the last two weeks, their lead running back “looks better than the last two Mondays.”
With Warren as the featured back and lead piece on offense, the Steelers have an identity. The offensive line continues to look better, and their reliance on combo blocks and an aggressive demeanor only helps Warren’s game.
If they keep this going, the Steelers are in a good place offensively. Quarterback Aaron Rodgers looks strong over three straight games, and they’ve posted 30 points in back-to-back home games.
It seems like Mike McCarthy is making the right call with Jaylen Warren.

title: Steelers vs. Colts Grades: Offense and Coaching Shine
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Pittsburgh Steelers went to war with the Indianapolis Colts. Both organizations were looking for their third victory of the season, but the Steelers left Acrisure Stadium victorious.
The Steelers out together an impressive win over the Colts, defeating them by a final score of 34-22.
It was a winning effort from the Steelers, but how impressive were they in victory? Riding high after their third home win of the season, this is how the Steelers' Week 5 performance grades out
There was tons to like about the offense, which was undoubtedly the best piece of the Steelers in Week 5.
Aaron Rodgers etched his name in Pittsburgh franchise history, joining Terry Bradshaw and Ben Roethlisberger as the only quarterbacks to record three touchdown passes in three consecutive games or more. He finished Week 5 22/31 for 235 yards and three touchdowns.
Even better news exiting the game was the offensive line keeping Rodgers protected. They only allowed one sack in Week 5 and gave Rodgers plenty of time and space in the pocket.
The star of the game, once again, was running back Jaylen Warren. With 15 carries for 101 yards, plus six receptions for 87 yards and an additional score, Warren was an unstoppable force against the Colts. He broke off a 50-yard run for one of his touchdowns, and took a screen pass 87 yards to the house for another.
Rookie wide receiver Germie Bernard had the biggest game of his young career as well. Without Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson exiting the game at halftime, Bernard was a frequent target. He finished the game with six receptions for 80 yards on nine targets.
The biggest win of the day for the defense was how they shut down star running back Jonathan Taylor. One of the premier runners in the NFL, the Steelers limited him to less than 50 yards on the ground.
It wasn't a perfect day for the defense, however. They allowed 267 passing yards to quarterback Daniel Jones while only getting him once in the backfield. They also failed to contain tight end Tyler Warren, who posted seven receptions for 83 yards on nine targets.
In the end, the Steelers did enoug defensively to get the victory. But for another week, the defense has had some serious flaws exposed.
Chris Boswell had a bounce back game, hitting both field goals he attempted in Week 5. That included a long of 54 yards and it put the Steelers in front by 12 points in the final moments of the contest.
Punter Cameron Johnson was rock solid in his work as well. He punted three times, posting an average of 52.0 yards per punt.
Even rookie Kaden Wetjen had a good day in the return game. On five kick-off return attempts, he posted 110 yards, good for an average of 22.0 per return.
The Steelers couldn't ask for much more from their special teamsin the win.
You can't be critical of this staff's performance in Week 5. Sure, there were things to clean up, but this was an excellent response to the Week 4 stinker they left.
Head coach Mike McCarthy called a great game offensively, but Patrick Graham moving from the booth to the sideline was a big difference maker. Maybe it was a placebo effect, but the communication was much smoother and well-mannered in Week 5 compared to Week 4.

title: Steelers Need to Sign a WR
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Pittsburgh Steelers need wide receiver help. Only a day ago, everyone was talking about this team not needing to look at the wide receiver trade market because of their young talent. Today, the group is depleted, and they desperately need help.
With the news that Roman Wilson is set to miss multiple weeks with a finger injury, the Steelers are left with DK Metcalf and Germie Bernard as their starters. Michael Pittman Jr. is on Injured Reserve with a foot injury, and Ben Skowronek also left Week 5 against the Indianapolis Colts, dealing with a calf injury.
So, right now, Pittsburgh's room is Metcalf, Bernard and rookie Kaden Wetjen. Wetjen is primarily a returner and hasn't played an offensive snap yet.
The team will likely call up Brandon Smith from the practice squad. Smith didn't record a catch against the Colts but was a training camp standout and a player Aaron Rodgers has shared his faith in multiple times.
"Well, B-Smith hasn't taken a ton of offensive reps. I've been around him for a few years. He was with us in New York, and always enjoyed him being on the fieldand his ability. I think he's a talented guy," Rodgers said after the Colts game.
"But we can play in 12 all day long, and if we need to, we will. But I was really proud of Germ the way he stepped in. There were a couple of plays with B-Smith. Like we had this play we're running inside zone, and we have this short motion to block the safety. Just by the end of the week it was just assumed that motion. I wasn't even calling it.
"I looked over, and I was, like, Oh, B has probably never done this. I was, like, Hey. He didn't know what I was thinking.
"So we were kind of making it up a little bit as we went there, but I'm proud of B-Smith. He's a smart guy and knows his stuff, and he'll be ready to take on a bigger role this week, I’m sure."
The team will likely need to explore their outside options, though. The name everyone will immediately think of is Tyreek Hill, but he's not the only veteran on the market. Two even have ties to the Steelers. And it'll come down to how big of a role the coaching staff is looking to fill with a signing.
If Mike McCarthy wants another starter-level player in the mix, Hill is the name to watch out for. The six-time All-Pro is 32-years-old and looking to play this season after suffering a dislocated knee in 2025. But he claims he's healthy, and if he is, he's easily the biggest name on the market.
If the Steelers are simply looking for a contributor to play behind Metcalf and Bernard , and in the mix with Smith, Skowronek and Wetjen, there are other names.
JuJu Smith-Schuster hasn't played in Pittsburgh since 2021, but spent the first five years of his career wearing the black and gold. The physical receiver is mostly a slot option at this point in his career, but could be a reliable set of hands for short-yardage situations and over the middle passes.
Gabe Davis is recovering from an ACL and may not be ready to play. But at 27 years old, he may be worth making a phone call to to check on his health heading into Week 6.
And then there are others; Ray-Ray McCloud is a player the Steelers' organization knows well. Curtis Samuel is somewhat of a mystery free agent, and maybe the biggest surprise to not be on a roster or practice squad somewhere. Mecole Hardman, Justin Watson, Josh Reynolds and others are still available as well.
It'll come down to Pittsburgh's perference. Whether or not they're looking for a bigger name or a fill-in while they wait for Wilson and Pittman Jr. How long they truly expect both to be out could play a significant role in their decision.
We don't know who yet, but expect someone. The Steelers certainly need another wide receiver before Week 6.

title: Steelers Bringing Back Hard-Hitting LB
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Pittsburgh Steelers are set to bring in veteran linebacker Elandon Roberts with the intention of re-signing the 32-year-old, according to Steelers Now's Alan Saunders.
Roberts spent the end of training camp with the Steelers, rejoining the defense and defensive coordinator Patrick Graham, who coached him with the Las Vegas Raiders the year prior. He was the biggest surprise release of the final 53-man roster, being surpassed by Patrick Queen, Payton Wilson, Cole Holcomb and Carson Bruener in the final cuts.
Now, Roberts is set to return to the Steelers, where his presence is needed. Both Queen and Wilson have been under heavy criticism throughout the season for failing to be reliable inside linebacker options. Their struggles have shown the most in run support, which is where Roberts thrives.
It's unknown if Roberts will sign to the active roster or practice squad when he does ink a deal with the Steelers. Chances are, even if he does sign with the practice squad initially, the intention will be to bring him up to the active roster at some point.
Roberts is entering his 11th NFL season, starting 121 games and recording 694 tackles, 14.5 sacks and 60 tackles for loss.
The Steelers defense is trying to figure out their flaws as they approach the midway point of the season, but it's becoming more and more clear that their lack of talent at the inside linebacker room can't be solved without adding to the group. Queen and Wilson have spurts of quality play, but overall, both have struggled more than they've succeeded for the Steelers.
Meanwhile, Cole Holcomb hasn't been a reliable backup and has become more of a special teams contributor than defensive help.
Roberts should be able to come into the Steelers' lineup and help immediately. Whether he joins the starting group or not, his presence in the run game is something Pittsburgh desperately needs. His drive as a starter will also help, and his leadership is also something they can utilize as they try to keep things on track.
How the Steelers create a roster spot for Roberts is up in the air. Bruener is a key special teams contributor and will likely remain in that role for his second season. Holcomb could be a bubble player if the Steelers chose to replace their depth.
If not, Queen and Wilson are the names to watch. And with a starter-level player joining the group, anything is on the table.

title: Steelers Get Bad News on Roman Wilson's Injury
full_text:
The Pittsburgh Steelers look like they're about to lose another one of their top wide receivers for a sustained period of time.
According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler, Roman Wilson is expected to be out for a few weeks after suffering a finger injury at the end of the first half of the Steelers' Week 5 win over the Indianapolis Colts.
"Steelers WR Roman Wilson is expected to miss a couple of weeks due to a finger injury suffered Sunday, per source," Fowler wrote on X . "He’s still gathering info and seeking a second opinion."
Steelers WR Roman Wilson is expected to miss a couple of weeks due to a finger injury suffered Sunday, per source. He’s still gathering info and seeking a second opinion.
Pittsburgh is dealing with significant injury concerns across the board at wide receiver.
Michael Pittman Jr. was placed on the reserve/injured list on October 10 after aggravating his foot injury last week. The 29-year-old, who originally missed the team's Week 2 game against the New England Patriots, is dealing with plantar fasciitis and won't be back on the field until Week 10 at the absolute earliest.
Alongside Wilson, Ben Skowronek sustained a calf injury in the first half against Indianapolis and missed the rest of the contest from that point forward.
DK Metcalf, Germie Bernard and Kaden Wetjen are the only healthy receivers remaining on the 53-man roster. Brandon Smith was also active against the Colts, though he was a practice squad elevation .
The obvious short-term solution for the Steelers is to sign Smith to the 53-man roster.
The 27-year-old training camp standout played 16 snaps on offense vs. Indianapolis and has two practice squad elevations left, but there's now an opening for him on the 53-man roster.
Wetjen is strictly a kick returner and has yet to see the field on offense as a rookie, though, so Pittsburgh will have to make another move or two at receiver now that Wilson seems set to miss multiple games.
Bernard proved that he can start next to Metcalf by posting 80 yards on six catches against the Colts, and the Steelers have the luxury of being able to run a ton of 12 personnel with Pat Freiermuth and Darnell Washington at tight end, but they still need another real option at receiver.
Whether it's making an early trade nearly a month before the November 10 trade deadline or bringing in a veteran free agent, Pittsburgh has to get aggressive and be extremely diligent in filling its hole at receiver in the coming days.

title: 7 Winners, 3 Losers From Steelers Win Over Colts
full_text:
The Pittsburgh Steelers are back in the win column .
At Acrisure Stadium, the Steelers came away with a 34-22 victory over the Indianapolis Colts that moves them to 3-2 on the season heading into a Week 6 matchup with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Here are seven winners and three losers for Pittsburgh in its first two-score win of the season.
On a day where their wide receiver depth was greatly tested , Freiermuth really stepped up as a weapon in the passing game for Rodgers.
After having just 17 yards and a touchdown in Week 4 against the Cleveland Browns, Freiermuth finished with two scores and 44 yards on five catches in Pittsburgh's win over the Colts.
It was his first multi-touchdown performance since Week 7 last season against the Cincinnati Bengals.
With Michael Pittman Jr. (foot) having been placed on the reserve/injured list while Roman Wilson (hand) and Ben Skowronek (calf) each didn't play in the second half with their injuries, the Steelers needed Bernard more than ever in this contest.
The second-round pick more than held up his end of the bargain, posting six catches for 80 yards and being a constant force in the middle of the field.
Frazier had been the bright spot of the Steelers' offensive line coming into this week, but he had an uneven showing vs. Indianapolis.
Frazier gave up a sack, which was his first of the season according to Pro Football Focus , and he was also called for a holding penalty on what would've been a first-down catch by Brandon Smith in the third quarter.
In his third-straight game commanding nearly all of the touches out of the backfield with Rico Dowdle out due to a toe injury, Warren continued his run of dominance this week.
His first touchdown went for 80 yards on a reception on Pittsburgh's second drive of the day in the first quarter, and he later broke off a 50-yard rushing touchdown in the third quarter.
When it was all said and done, Warren logged 101 yards on 15 carries to go with six receptions for 87 yards in the win.
There was some hope that Metcalf was trending in the right direction after putting up 115 yards vs. Cleveland last week.
Against the Colts, however, he was extremely quiet. Metcalf had only three catches for 12 yards, which was his lowest single-game output in the latter category since the Steelers' win over Indianapolis in Week 9 last season.
Rodgers was not sharp in the Steelers' Week 4 loss to the Browns, though he bounced back against the Colts.
The 42-year-old opened the game 11-of-11 for 116 yards and two touchdowns, and he closed the day with 235 yards and three touchdowns on 22-of-31 passing.
Rodgers was in command the entire way through, and it helped lead to Pittsburgh's highest point total in a single game since Week 11 of the 2025 campaign.
The Steelers had just one sack in this game, which belonged to Cam Heyward.
That doesn't mean Highsmith wasn't giving Colts left tackle Bernhard Raimann fits though, as he finished with a season-high four pressures (per Pro Football Focus ).
Queen has been a liability all year long for Pittsburgh at inside linebacker, and that didn't change in this contest.
According to SumerSports, Queen allowed three receptions on three targets in coverage for 36 yards while also missing a tackle ( per PFF ) and not contributing much against the run.
Samuel Jr. turned in what was arguably his best game for Pittsburgh up to this point.
Down Jamel Dean, who was inactive due to an ankle injury, Samuel Jr. posted four pass breakups (including multiple in the end zone) while allowing only 36 yards and three catches on 11 targets in coverage (per SumerSports ).

title: Steelers' Aaron Rodgers Honors Mike Tomlin After Win Over Colts
full_text:
Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers made sure to shout out his former head coach after the team's 34-22 Week 5 victory over the Indianapolis Colts .
In his postgame press conference , Rodgers was wearing a shirt that read "DGBTTF", which means "don't get beat to the flat."
The future Hall of Famer was asked whether that was a coincidence or a warning to the Colts' defense, and Rodgers explained that it was "an ode" to Tomlin since he often used that phrase.
"No it's not a warning," Rodgers said. "It's an ode to Mike T. He used to always say, 'don't get beat to the flat.'"
Rodgers has been rather hold and cold for the Steelers in his final season before retirement.
The 42-year-old was really solid against the Atlanta Falcons and Cincinnati Bengals in Week 1 and 3, respectively, while going through some struggles in Weeks 2 and 4 vs. the New England Patriots and Cleveland Browns, respectively.
The common denominator for a strong outing from Rodgers has been good pass protection up front from Pittsburgh's offensive line. He was sacked five times against the Browns and didn't have much time to operate, which played a big role in how inconsistent he was, but the unit really clutched up vs. Indianapolis.
Rodgers was sacked just one time, and he had plenty of time to sit around in the pocket and find his receivers all throughout the contest.
He started the day 11-of-11, and he finished the game with 235 yards on 22-of-31 passing for three touchdowns and no interceptions.
As a result, Rodgers helped lead the Steelers to their first two-score victory of the season and their first since Week 15 of the 2025 campaign.
Without Michael Pittman Jr., who was placed on IR with his foot injury ahead of this contest, while both Roman Wilson (hand) and Ben Skowronek (calf) didn't play in the second half due to their injuries, Pittsburgh needed a collective effort on offense in order to come out with a win over the Colts.
From Rodgers being sharp to the likes of Jaylen Warren, Pat Freiermuth and Germie Bernard all having banner days as the offensive line won most of their battles against Indianapolis' defensive front, the Steelers got perhaps their most complete performance of the year across the board in this one.
They'll have to keep it up moving forward if they want to remain in the hunt for another AFC North title or a Wild Card spot, but it's certainly a huge step in the right direction.

title: Steelers vs. Colts Takeaways: Offense Just Exploded
full_text:
PITTSBURGH -- The Pittsburgh Steelers move to 3-2 on the season and regroup in a big way after a loss to the Cleveland Browns. Leaving Acrisure Stadium for the third time in 2026, the Steelers defeat the Indianapolis Colts 34-22, moving to 3-0 at home this year.
The game wasn't the smoothest victory for the Steelers, but they seemed to be in control from start to finish. Jaylen Warren put the team on his back from start to finish, just like he has throughout the season. Aaron Rodgers helped, though, adding three touchdowns of his own.
This team remains a mixed bag, but one with a winning record. They'll take it.
Opening up the notebook afterward, there are plenty of takeaways that stand out. Let's dive into them.
How many times do these takeaways need to include Jaylen Warren before it becomes too normal for him to play the way he has been. Warren may not just be the best player on the Steelers' offense this season, but the best player on their team.
Warren got things started for the Steelers with an 80-yard touchdown catch-and-run on the opening play of the offense's second drive. Aaron Rodgers got drilled as he dumped it off to Warren, who took it to the outside, beat the defense and took off down the sideline.
In the second half, he got things moving with a 50-yard touchdown run up the middle to give Pittsburgh a 24-16 lead.
He's the first player in the NFL to have an 80-yard touchdown reception and a 50-yard touchdown run in the same game since Herschel Walker did it for the Dallas Cowboys in Week 15 of the 1986 season.
Warren finished the first half with 81 receiving yards and 13 rushing yards on four carries. He finished the day with 101 rushing yards, 87 receiving yards and two touchdowns.
Warren remains one of the best running backs in the NFL and continues to climb up that list. He's playing at an All-Pro level and is keeping Pittsburgh's offense alive in crucial moments. Whether it's being a reliable checkdown or the player who needs to carry the offense through the ground, he's there to be a force.
The Steelers need this to continue, but they also need to be cautious about keeping him healthy. When you have a player as impactful as Warren is, you need to treat them like the superstar they are - and the key piece to the team's success that he is.
Side note: Rodgers' pass to Warren was also history. He tied Ben Roethlisberger for the most career touchdown passes of 80 yards or more with nine.
Jaylen Warren is on a whole other level this season pic.twitter.com/DZ9YDmnLPG
The Steelers need to fix their special teams. Kaden Wetjen isn't exciting but was selected in the fourth round to be a star kick returner. Chris Boswell is missing field goals, including a few before the game, which brought just as much concern as missing them in-game. And somehow, coverage for kickoffs and punts has gotten worse by the week.
The special teams unit as a whole is bad, right now.
It's hard to identify where the changes need to be made, and what's more concerning that is there are some big names within this group in terms of special teams recognition. Ben Skowronek, Jack Sawyer, Travis Homer, Brandin Echols and Cole Holcomb are players known around the league for their special teams play. This season, they aren't getting it done, most of the time.
This group needs to improve or they're going to cost this team games. And Danny Crossman should be feeling the pressure for how poorly his group has performed.
Side note again: This is all outside of Cameron Johnston, who has been phenomenal all season. He's playing like the punter the Steelers have been trying to find for the last 20 years.
Sometimes, Aaron Rodgers is Aaron Rodgers. He did it in the first game of the season, putting on a show against the Atlanta Falcons. He did it again against the Indianapolis Colts, and it's always fun to watch.
At 42-years-old, Rodgers was more mobile than he's been in a while and on multiple occassions extended the play with his legs, finding open receivers after leaving the pocket and keeping his eyes down field.
He was accurate, collected and outside of one missed pass to Pat Freiermuth, there weren't many moments when you were thinking he made a poor play or poor decision.
Hoopin' @AaronRodgers12 | @oti_germie pic.twitter.com/7qWJG3k5hi
It was a nice reminder that the Steelers do have a legendary quarterback running the show. He doesn't always have the ability to win with his physical traits, but whenever he's feeling good, he can do some magical things.
This was one of those games where the Steelers know if he plays this well, they have a good shot to win.
The Steelers haven't fixed anything in their secondary despite changing, well, nothing. This team tried to give Asante Samuel Jr. another chance, and maybe they plan on giving him more, but he may not be the answer. Right now, he can't stop anyone or any route. He's the biggest liability on the field for the Steelers, but he's not the only one.
Everyone outside of Jalen Ramsey wasn't on their A-game against the Colts. Daylen Everette didn't play terribly, but he couldn't keep up on every route. Jaquan Brisker continues to go backward instead of forward, and the team has lost so much faith in Rayshawn Jenkins that he didn't play - and Robert Spears-Jennings barely took any snaps to replace him.
When he was on the field, he spent a lot of time pre-snap telling people where to be. That's a seventh-round rookie telling veterans where to be.
It's time for the Steelers to listen to Jalen Ramsey and get Sean Murphy-Bunting on the field. Brandin Echols should also be an option, and it's pretty surprising that he hasn't been. This team needs to find a solution to the opposite side of Everrette/Jamel Dean.
They also need to figure out Brisker, though. The local star has been a liability in coverage over the last few weeks and is seemingly getting further behind by the game. Maybe he just needs DeShon Elliott back to support him, but something needs to be figured out.
The Steelers lost Roman Wilson right at the end of the first half after he suffered a hand injury. How quickly the team ruled him out for the game raises concerns, and if Wilson is set to miss time because of the injury, he leaves Pittsburgh with two starters - DK Metcalf and Germie Bernard.
He wasn't alone, though. Ben Skowronek left the game with a calf injury and was unable to return. It's unknown what he's exactly dealing with and if he'll miss time as well.
That leaves the Steelers with Metcalf, Bernard and Kaden Wetjen. That's their only three healthy wide receivers on the active roster. Brandon Smith is expected to be called up to help off of the practice squad.
That's not enough, even with Smith. This team needs to add help immediately. Maybe they start by seeing if Wetjen can be part of the offense and if Smith is good enough to contribute consistently. Brandon Johnson is another veteran on their practice squad they can utilize.
Names like Tyreek Hill, JuJu Smith-Schuster and Gabe Davis may need to be on their radar leaving this game, though.

title: Steelers WR Situation Gets Worse After Roman Wilson Injury
full_text:
One of the Pittsburgh Steelers ' top wide receivers suffered an injury at the end of the first half that will keep him out for the remainder of the team's Week 5 game against the Indianapolis Colts.
On one of the final plays of the second quarter, Aaron Rodgers attempted an 11-yard pass to Roman Wilson that was initially ruled complete at Indianapolis' 19-yard line.
It was subsequently reviewed and overturned to incomplete, though that wasn't the most important development to come out of the play for the Steelers.
Wilson has seen grabbing his wrist/hand as he headed to the sideline, and he was later ruled out for the remainder of the contest with a hand injury.
Before departing the game, Wilson had not recorded a catch, and the play on which he got hurt was his only target as well.
With Ben Skowronek also having been ruled out due to a calf injury while Michael Pittman Jr. was placed on the reserve/injured list with his foot injury on October 10, the Steelers now have a complete lack of depth at wide receiver.
DK Metcalf and Germie Bernard will have to do most of the heavylifting for Pittsburgh the rest of the way against the Colts.
The Steelers will likely also lean quite a bit on 12-personnel packages in which Pat Freiermuth and Darnell Washington are on the field at the same time as a means of making up for their deficiency at receiver.
Pittsburgh elevated training camp standout Brandon Smith from its practice squad after placing Pittman Jr. on IR, though Kaden Wetjen is the only other healthy receiver on the team's 53-man roster.
While the Steelers can get through the rest of their matchup vs. the Colts without much of a depth chart at receiver, their long-term standing at the position depends on the severity of Wilson and Skowronek's injuries.
Because Pittman Jr. will be forced to miss at least three more contests beyond this week, Pittsburgh was already in the market to make a move at receiver.
If Wilson and Skowronek have to miss any additional time with their injuries, the team would then be further incentivized to make an addition.
Perhaps Smith could sign to the 53-man roster if that ends up being the case, though there could also be more transactions on the horizon.

title: 3 Risers and Fallers After Seahawks' Week 5 Loss vs 49ers
full_text:
The Seattle Seahawks (3-2) suffered another ugly loss thanks to careless turnovers and poor performances at key spots. Seattle had five turnovers, but still had a chance to take down their divisional rival, the San Francisco 49ers. Instead, Seattle has to take a short week of disappointment and use it to prepare for the Denver Broncos (3-2).
​The Seahawks have a couple of players they can turn to in this short week and build off their success. There are also players the Seahawks have to be prepared to make changes in their roster moving forward.
​There were plenty of great performances from several Seahawks players. Among the players who have earned a bump in roles is third-year cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett . He was among the standout cornerbacks for Seattle. He played great defensively and on special teams . His memorable moment was delivering a solid hit on a punt to force a fumble and give the Seahawks a turnover.
During the offseason, defensive tackle Byron Murphy II ensured he was good enough to be a Pro Bowl selection and to account for 10 sacks this 2026 NFL Season. Murphy got closer quickly with a standout game against the 49ers.
Murphy accounted for his second and third sack of the season on Sunday . He easily had his best performance so far, with six total tackles, five solo tackles, three quarterback hits, two sacks and three tackles for loss. He might be able to fulfill his promise.
Remember when there was panic heading into the season over kicker Jason Myers? That panic should be cold and silent after Sunday’s big performance. Myers was 5-of-5 in field goals and made two more extra points, totaling 17 points for Seattle. He made at least five of his field goals for the sixth time in his professional career . While the Seahawks’ offense was unstable, Myers was reliable.​
​This section shouldn’t be a debate for all 12. The first player in this section and should likely be demoted is running back George Holani . Through the five games played this season, Holani has rushed for 77 yards on 26 carries. In the 49ers loss, he had two inexcusable fumbles.
His best asset, which is pass protection, was heavily exposed and was overworked at times by the 49ers' defense. It has now reached a point where Holani might be too much of a liability to keep on the 53-man roster and needs to be replaced.
​Holani isn’t the only running back that the 12 are tired of seeing. Veteran Emanuel Wilson continues to be a lack of spark for the Seahawks’ running game. Wilson rushed for 61 yards and a touchdown on 20 carries, but his fumble deep in Seahawks’ territory helped give the 49ers another touchdown.
The 12 are tired of Wilson, a power back, being utilized as the No. 1 option, but he may be all the Seahawks get until rookie Jadarian Price or veteran Zach Charbonnet come back.
There might be some competition at first-string cornerback coming soon if not only is Pritchett playing at a high level, but also if Josh Jobe continues to struggle. Jobe, arguably, had his worst game as a member of the Seahawks.
Jobe struggled enormously against 49ers veteran wide receiver Mike Evans. Jobe allowed seven catches for 1112 yards, one touchdown and a passer rating of 155.6. The Seahawks have Pritchett and veteran Trevon Diggs to take over if Jobe continuously struggles.
