title: Grading Every Titans Position Group After Week 5 Loss vs. Texans
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans produced another lifeless effort on Sunday, falling 26-3 to the Houston Texans in a lopsided battle between two winless teams.
Even the most optimistic Titans fan can’t help but feel dejected after a performance like that . Things started badly, and they only got worse as the game progressed.
This Titans team is simply broken in many ways, and until things get fixed, you’re going to continue seeing the type of poor grades you’re about to sees
QB Cam Ward struggled mightily in this one, completing just 23 of his 36 passes for 170 yards and one interception.
The second-year quarterback continues to be erratic with his ball placement. Ward has a knack for making catches harder than they have to be, which leads to drops or missed opportunities after the catch.
Another area where he continues to struggle is his ability to process what he’s seeing both pre- and post-snap. His inability to diagnose the moving puzzle often gets him in trouble and/or prevents him from hitting the big plays that are there to be made.
All of these issues showed up early and often in what was arguably Ward’s worst outing of the season. But considering the performance of the offensive line (we’ll touch on that later), I’ll at least spare him from the F.
Things got off to a rocky start and never get much better. RB Tyjae Spears fumbled in the first quarter and failed to record a single rushing yard, while RB Tony Pollard averaged less than four yards per carry.
It was a putrid afternoon all around, and the inability to get anything going on the ground was a big reason why.
The receiver group of Carnell Tate, Wan’Dale Robinson, Elic Ayomanor, Calvin Ridley, and Chimere Dike combined for just 137 yards on 13 catches.
There were a couple of big plays left on the table, most notably a couple of missed opportunities to Tate that failed to connect because of poor execution and/or penalties. But aside from that, it was a rather lifeless performance by the entire passing attack.
Where do we even begin with this one?
I would say this was an absolutely atrocious performance by the offensive line, but that would somehow be downplaying how bad it really was. The offensive line allowed a combined 20 pressures, three sacks, and two hits on the day.
LT Dan Moore was the biggest culprit, allowing eight of those pressures for an absurd pressure rate of 19.5 percent.
Watching this play in slow-motion with this music is *chefs kiss* pic.twitter.com/OvC0NYFbzI
It was a long afternoon for the group upfront, and the point total on the scoreboard directly reflects that.
It was another largely irrelevant day for a group that hasn’t contributed much. The group of Gunnar Helm, Daniel Bellinger, and Kylen Granson combined for just five yards.
The latter of whom had the opportunity for a big play early in the game, but he was unable to reel in the pass, and it became another missed opportunity for a team that’s had more than its fair share.
It was a rather mediocre outing for a group that has actually played well for most of the year. The group combined for eight pressures and six run stops. DT Jeffery Simmons led the way with three pressures, while DL Jordan Elliott topped the group with two run stops.
But for the Titans to win, they need their defensive line to be a dominant front, and that just wasn’t the case here.
Cody Barton, Cedric Gray, and Anthony Hill Jr. had a solid game for the most part. The three of them were credited with 17 combined tackles, multiple pressures, and half a sack (Gray).
They also helped play a key role in holding the Texans’ ground game to under three yards per carry.
The Titans’ secondary entered the game very thin on the backend, and it only got worse. S Amani Hooker was ruled out with a concussion, while S Kevin Winston Jr. left early with a quadriceps injury, and their absence was felt throughout the contest.
The Texans’ group of pass catchers combined for 261 yards and one touchdown on 26 catches.

title: Postgame Quotes That Matter From Robert Saleh After Titans' Lifeless Week 5 Loss to Texans
full_text:
Another Sunday means another Tennessee Titans loss. This time, head coach Robert Saleh's group fell to the Houston Texans 26-3 at home, dropping to 0-5 in the 2026 season.
Not much went right for Tennessee against Houston. The offense managed just 187 total yards and didn't find the end zone, while the defense allowed Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud to get too comfortable in the pocket, leading to an efficient outing for the 2023 No. 2 overall pick.
The Titans are arguably the worst team in the NFL and have shown no improvement from last season's 3-14 performance. Saleh spoke to the media after his team's latest embarrassing loss, and it's clear that he is running out of answers.
Though he isn't the sole reason for Sunday's loss to the Texans, quarterback Cam Ward still didn't play very well . The 2025 No. 1 overall pick completed 23 of 36 passes for 170 yards and threw an interception.
After another uninspiring performance from his young signal-caller, Saleh was asked about the possibility of benching Ward for veteran Mitchell Trubisky, and the Titans head coach made it known that Ward is still Tennessee's No. 1 quarterback.
"Cam's our starting quarterback," Saleh said. "We're going to give him every opportunity to be successful this year, and we're going to continue working with him, grinding with him and trying to help him get better."
Ward was also asked why he should remain the Titans' QB1, and the Miami product said he is more than capable of handling the responsibilities of being an NFL starting quarterback.
"I just think my process, what I'm willing to sacrifice every week to get to the player that I want to be," Ward said on remaining as the Titans starting quarterback. "Also the player that the team needs and the organization needs to win games. I love the criticism and everything that comes with the quarterback territory. It's the best position in the world. Stuff goes the right way, you take all the credit. Stuff goes the wrong way, you take all the blame."
He hasn't lived up to expectations so far this year, but it is still too early to bench Ward. Tennessee must give Ward an ample sample size before making a decision on whether he is the answer at the most pivotal position in the sport.
Despite a 0-5 start to his tenure as head coach, Saleh isn't losing any confidence. The defensive-minded coach stated that he will turn the Titans around and bring the franchise back into the sun as a winning organization.
"We are going to flip this thing, and eventually this organization is going to have its day in the sun," Saleh said.
Tennessee has won six games since the start of the 2024 season, and hasn't tallied a victory since Week 16 of the 2025 season. There may not be a franchise in a darker place than the Titans right now, and we'll see whether Saleh can turn the tide and be the coach who brings winning football back to Nashville.
The most impactful quote from Saleh's press conference was his message to his guys about the next 12 games. Saleh said that the final 12 games of the year will decide who will stick around in Tennessee and be a part of the franchise turnaround.
"The next 12 games will determine which of you will be here when we turn this thing around."
The Titans were one of the most active franchises in the league on the player acquisition front this past offseason. So far, none of those additions have paid off and made major contributions. We could see another roster turnover period for Tennessee as soon as next spring.
A road contest against the 2-3 Indianapolis Colts is next for the Titans. A loss would drop Tennessee to 0-6 for the first time since 2009, and could officially kickstart draft talk.

title: Titans QB Cam Ward's Promising Progress Stalls In 26-3 Loss vs. Texans
full_text:
All of the optimism surrounding QB Cam Ward went out the window on Sunday. The Titans' signal caller had arguably his worst outing of the season, completing 23 of his 36 passes for 170 yards and one interception. It certainly wasn't all his fault that the team only produced three points.
Ward was sacked four times and was under duress throughout the contest, largely due to LT Dan Moore Jr. having a horrendous performance on Sunday. Truthfully, the entire offense looked overmatched on a day where a fellow 0-4 team stood across from them.
Look at my franchise’s left tackle… pic.twitter.com/mhBxrYeMWW
The Titans shot themselves in the foot far too many times to have a realistic chance in this one. This team doesn’t have the talent or experience to overcome those types of mistakes.
At one point, they had four straight drives in the first half that resulted in a three-and-out, a fumble, an interception, and another three-and-out.
To take their struggles a step further, Tennessee only produced 108 total yards of offense through the first three quarters, ultimately ending the game with just 187 in total.
While things haven’t necessarily been as bad as they were on Sunday, they haven’t exactly been much better. The former first overall pick is now 3-19 as a starter and has just five total touchdowns and four turnovers through the first five games.
Now that another lifeless loss is in the rearview mirror, Ward was bluntly asked why he deserves to continue being the Titans’ quarterback long term.
“ I just think my process. What I’m willing to sacrifice each and every week to get to the player that I want to be, but also the player that the team needs, and the organization needs to win games. I love the criticism. I love everything that comes with the quarterback territory. At the end of the day, it’s the best position in the world. ( When ) stuff goes the right way, you take all the credit, and when stuff goes the wrong way, you take all the blame. I know I’m capable of this position. I have the right guys around me to uplift me, and myself to uplift them. And we’ll eventually put it together .”
Coaches and teammates continue to rave about Ward behind the scenes and the amount of work he puts in. However, It’s clear that Ward’s effort inside the building isn’t carrying over to the games. The second-year quarterback was asked why he thinks that is.
“ We just gotta continue to have urgency. I think we have that each and every week, but at the end of the day, we just gotta make plays. I have to make plays. The whole team has to make plays. That’s what it comes down to — making plays. ”
Ward was then asked what this team could do to start fixing these seemingly never-ending problems and how much blame he puts on himself for the issues at hand
“ I just try to continue to do my job. At the end of the day, I have a lot of stuff to continue to get better at. I think that’s gonna put us in position to win games… But everyone in the building knows it’s going to take all 11 of us on offense to get things how we want it. But as far as my job, there’s still a lot of things I have to clean up. I have to continue to motivate my guys the way they need to be motivated. I have to continue to lead with my style. I think if we keep doing that, if we keep on making progress forward, the wins will eventually come .”
One thing is for certain, Tennessee needs better production from their young quarterback they invested so much in. If Ward starts to figure things out and he starts to play well, the wins will follow.
But if they don’t, the Titans might need to have some uncomfortable conversations this offseason.

title: What’s Next For The Robert Saleh-Led Titans After Falling to 0-5
full_text:
The Robert Saleh era in Tennessee hasn’t exactly gotten off to the start many hoped for when he was hired.
After another lopsided loss, his team now sits at 0-5 on the year, which is a low not even former coaches Brian Callahan and Ken Whisenhunt can relate to. This is now the Titans’ worst start to a season since starting 0-6 back in 2009.
Now, if you want to remain optimistic, the Titans drastically turned that season around. They went on to win their next five in a row and nearly snuck into the playoffs at 8-8.
Unfortunately, this team doesn’t have anything close to what former RB Chris Johnson was doing that year. To put it bluntly: realistic chances of a turnaround for this Titans team are slim to none.
The Titans have now lost 44 of their last 56 games dating back to 2023. And to make matters worse, second-year QB Cam Ward has regressed to the point where many have become skeptical about his long-term future with the franchise.
The Miami product was supposed to be the savior for a Titans team that desperately needed one. Instead, he looks like a quarterback who is completely in over his head at the moment. That certainly doesn’t mean things can’t improve over time, but considering the product this fanbase has been forced to watch the last few years, nobody can blame them for growing impatient.
The real question is how patient this franchise — a franchise that’s infamously lacked patience of late — is willing to be with their former first overall pick?
I do think there’s a world where the Titans try to go the ‘Bryce Young route’ by sitting him for a few weeks, but someone like Ward needs to play. The only way he’s going to reach his full potential is by getting the reps he needs.
Therefore, I have a hard time believing Ward will be benched any time soon, but if these types of ugly performances continue to stack up, then anything is possible.
Now that the playoffs appear to be an unrealistic goal, what happens to veteran players such as DT Jeffery Simmons, RB Tony Pollard, and WR Calvin Ridley?
Let’s start with the obvious blockbuster. Trading Simmons would undoubtedly net to a massive return that would surely include a first-round pick in the upcoming draft.
But for them to trade the one true star they have on this team, the return would have to be an offer they simply couldn’t refuse. And maybe they do get that from a desperate team that's willing to do anything to get over the hump.
But trading Simmons would undoubtedly be another crushing blow for a franchise that’s suffered far too many of them as of late. Without a king's ransom in return, I think he ends up staying in Tennessee as the face of the franchise heading into their fancy new stadium next year.
Every other veteran should be on the table. Rumors of Pollard drawing interest elsewhere should only grow as we get closer to the trade deadline. If/when they get a respectable offer for the veteran running back, that’s one deal they should make without hesitation.
Pollard is likely gone after this year either way, so it would be wise to get something in return while they still can. Someone with his production and resume could yield an early-to-mid-day three pick in return.
As for Ridley, the divorce between both parties is inevitable at the end of this year, so I have a hard time not envisioning Tennessee picking up the phone if someone calls about the veteran receiver.
With that said, given the age and recent production (or lack thereof) out of the Alabama product, don’t expect anything more than a late-round pick in return should somebody call.
Nonetheless, the fact that we’re talking about all this before Halloween is extremely disappointing. The Titans are clearly in the midst of another long season that has some fans already shifting their focus toward next year’s draft.
Many Titans fans are already salivating over the possibility of reuniting the former Buckeye tandem of Jeremiah Smith and Carnell Tate in Tennessee. However, that’s way down the line and they’ll need to do a lot more losing to make that happen.
But at the end of the day, that’s something for the fans to focus on. This team has to focus on blocking out the noise and continue trying to put their best foot forward regardless of the outcome on Sunday’s.
Only time will tell how all this plays out, but it’s clear that Saleh and his staff have a lot of work to do to get this team where they need to be.

title: Where to Watch and 2 Things to Expect: Titans Host 0-4 Texans in Battle for First Victory
full_text:
Neither the Tennessee Titans nor the Houston Texans have pulled out a win this season. Both teams sit in that bottom-of-the-barrel level of NFL teams who simply haven't figured it out yet.
Today, the division rivals will butt heads at Nissan Stadium. It's Cam Ward vs. C.J. Stroud. JC Latham vs. Will Anderson Jr. Robert Saleh vs. DeMeco Ryans - we'll touch on that matchup specifically.

Cam Ward set his season high in passing yards in Week 4, throwing for 222 through the air againt the Baltimore Ravens. We should be in for a similar performance, if not one more focused on the deep ball.
Ward has been criticized time and time again this season for failing to connect on explosive plays, along with OC Brian Daboll. Even in losing to the Ravens, however, Tennessee's offense finally opened up the passing game. Carnell Tate had 145 yards all by himself.
Against a so-far lackluster Texans secondary, the Titans are facing a must-win scenario coming off their best passing performance of the year. It'd be shocking for Ward and Daboll not to lean into that apparent advantage today.
With head coach DeMeco Ryans taking over play-calling duties for Houston's defense, two of the league's most storied DCs will coach against one another today. Saleh and Ryans have met one time prior as HCs, back in 2023.

Expect varied looks on either side of the ball, and even potentially turnovers both ways. The Texans certainly have the better offense on paper, but at least prior to Ryans taking over, the Titans' defense could easily be granted an edge here.
It'll be a real clash of the defensive titans on the sidelines, no pun intended. The victor in this duel could end up being the overall victor as a direct result.

title: Titans' Anthony Hill Jr. Slots Lower Than Expected in NFL.com's Rookie Defensive Rankings
full_text:
It's been a rough start to the year for the Tennessee Titans, as the team is 0-4 on the season and their playoff hopes are already basically dead. However, there have still been some bright spots in what has been a dreadful season so far, including linebacker Anthony Hill Jr.
Hill, Tennessee's second-round pick in April, has been a standout on head coach Robert Saleh's defense . The Texas product has tallied 42 tackles, 13 defensive stops, two pass deflections, and a 73.5 Pro Football Focus tackling grade.
Though Hill has experienced the usual rookie growing pains, especially in pass coverage, the 21-year-old has brought refreshing youth to the Titans' linebacker room. But it looks like some of the national media has yet to take full notice of Hill's solid performance.
NFL.com's Gennaro Filice released his rankings of the top rookie defenders in the NFL through four games, and Hill came in at No. 7. Sonny Styles of the Washington Commanders earned the top spot.
"As the Mike linebacker and green-dot wearer in Robert Saleh’s defense, Hill is automatically subject to reckless Fred Warner comparisons. I won’t be making any of those here, but the rookie does deserve shine for his sideline-to-sideline range. Over the first three weeks of the season, Hill piled up an NFL-high 34 tackles, earning him Defensive Rookie of the Month honors for September. Against the pass, he’s flashed ability as a blitzer but lacks consistency in coverage," Filice wrote of Hill.
Hill has played every single defensive snap for the Titans in 2026, and has held his own as a plus starter on the unit. Though the rookies above, including Styles, Arvell Reese of the New York Giants, Dillon Thieneman of the Chicago Bears, Mansoor Delane of the Kansas City Chiefs, Jacob Rodriguez of the Miami Dolphins, and Caleb Downs of the Dallas Cowboys, have shown their flashes, Hill has already established himself as one of the most pivotal pieces of Saleh's roster.
If Hill were on a winning team and playing like he has so far, the 6-foot-2 linebacker would be garnering more respect. However, with the Titans winless, it's hard to blame Filice for underrating Hill's production and output.
Tennessee will be eyeing their first win of the season against the Houston Texans at Nissan Stadium. Hill will need to patrol the middle of the field at a high level, make progress in pass coverage, and continue being tenacious in the run game for the Titans to finally exit a Sunday with a victory.

title: 2 Bold Predictions That Could Decide Titans' Divisional Matchup With Texans
full_text:
One day out of Week 5, the Tennessee Titans still appear to be facing an uphill battle against the division rival Houston Texans. Things haven't gotten any easier for the reigning worst team in the AFC South.
However, with the Texans also coming into this game at 0-4, the Titans have reason to be slightly more hopeful here. Robert Saleh did say that Houston may be "the greatest 0-4 team in the history of football," but the record doesn't lie. These two teams are entering Sunday's matchup on even ground.
I've got a handful of bold predictions for the Titans' duel. Either coming true could undoubtedly change the contest's outcome, and there's one to represent both sides of the ball.
If the Titans are to find a way to beat the Texans, their offense will have to find a way to keep up with C.J. Stroud. Coming off his best game of the 2026 season, I predict that Cam Ward will throw multiple touchdowns for the first time therein.
Ward wasn't perfect last week, but his 222 yards and chunk of deep-ball connections inspired a new home amongst Tennessee fans. The second-year QB looked more comfortable in Brian Daboll's system. He looked ready to take chances again.
The Texans are allowing an average of 260 passing yards per game this season. Head coach DeMeco Ryans taking over defensive play-calling duties could have an impact in either direction, but the unit as it has stood this year presents an open window for Ward.
If he's really going to take steps forward this year, there's no better time to prove it than Week 5. I believe Ward will give the home crowd in Nashville something to cheer about through the air.
Defensively, I'll also predict that both teams force a turnover. Both Saleh and Ryans are former defensive coordinators (and for the San Francisco 49ers, at that), and each calling plays against one another should up the ante on that side of the ball.
Tennessee and Houston have combined for just three interceptions on the season, but with disruptors like Will Anderson Jr. on one side and Jeffery Simmons on the other, we could see some loose balls on the ground.
Either way, I expect this one to get scrappy. Both teams are desperate for a victory. Saleh and Ryans are each backed against the wall, even if in different circumstances. It's a divisional game in which both franchises are trying to save themselves some embarrassment.
If I had to get specific, I'd say Tennessee turns it over through the air, and Houston on the ground. Stroud hasn't thrown an interception yet this year, though the Texans have four fumbles (two of them lost) on the season. Both were lost by Stroud.
It's a shot in the dark, but arguably no battle is harder to predict than one between two teams with nothing to lose. Expect the unexpected in Week 5, Titans fans.

title: Staff Predictions for Titans vs. Ravens: Tennessee Comes Out on Top for 1 Main Reason
full_text:
Last week, the Titans On SI staff predicted a Tennessee loss across the board against the Baltimore Ravens. Unfortunately, we turned out to be correct. The Titans fell in Week 4 to a score of 24-18, in a game that saw Brian Daboll's offense progress just below a breakthrough.
This week, our two picks tell a different story. In a pivotal AFC South matchup that will see one of the Titans and Texans secure your first win, we're predicting Tennessee's offense to tick in the right direction at the exact right time.
Robert Saleh just expressed his confidence that this Titans season is not over yet. "I feel if we can win one, we can build momentum," Saleh said. We expect Tennessee to finally make good on that opportunity this week.
I don't know why, but I've got a good feeling about this one. On paper, Tennessee winning their first game in Week 5 last year - after an 0-4 start - feels like a good omen. The Titans and Texans are also 24-24 all-time. For semantic reasons, Tennessee holding on to the series at home would be huge.
But Week 5 also looks to offer a few advantages for Tennessee. The Texans' passing defense has been among the least efficient in the league this season, and head coach DeMeco Ryans taking over play-calling duties could lead to a rough transitional period for Houston.
On the other hand, Cam Ward is coming off his best game of the season. With Carnell Tate good to go and the Titans playing their first game in Nashville in three weeks, the cards are quietly stacked up for a revenge game here.
The divisional stakes make it all the more important. Call me crazy, but I have the Titans in a narrow, offense-leading victory.
Although the Titans' offense is yet to crack 20 points, they have been forced to play in either extraordinary heat or rain in each of their four games this season. The weather in Nashville is expected to be 60s with a chance of sprinkles on Sunday, a welcomed change for the home team.
Houston's defense has been disappointing, giving up the sixth most points despite an elite pass rush. I anticipate big outings from WR Wan'Dale Robinson and WR Carnell Tate, as the Titans seek, and secure, their first victory of the season.

title: Titans Red Zone Report: Tennessee's Major Key to Scoring When it Matters vs. Texans
full_text:
So long as the Tennessee Titans continue to be one of the NFL's least efficient offenses, these red zone reports will continue to feel more like futuristic wishful thinking than anything else. Brian Daboll and Cam Ward have to find a way to get on the same page, and fast.
However, Week 4's loss at the hands of the Baltimore Ravens provided us with a one-drive sample size to properly diagnose the team's problems. The Titans found momentum in the second half, but Robert Saleh could have had his first win had one series of plays gone Tennessee's way.
Down 14-7 in the second quarter, the Titans were facing a first and goal in the red zone. We've already hit this issue numerous times, so I'll keep it short: Daboll ran Tony Pollard four straight times, Tennessee got stuffed on the goal line, and Baltimore scored in the other direction prior to halftime.
The Titans ultimately closed the gap to six points by the game's end - the difference between the team finding a way in on that pivotal drive in the second. In Week 5, it's all about trusting Ward's progression and betting on the guy under center.
Pollard is effective as a consistent, early-down veteran in an offense otherwise filled with rising young assets. Daboll using him as a four-down workhorse, however, is both predictable and terrible ineffective.
Daboll confirmed this week that he "felt good" about the looks for Pollard, refusing to express any outward regret on the plane ride home looking back on the incident. Again, though, the offense gave Ward the keys to open things up downfield after that.
Tennessee's comeback effort may have fallen short, but Ward would find Wan'Dale Robinson for a passing score in the first quarter. He'd then hit Carnell Tate in the end zone for a successful two-point conversion, too.
Of the Titans' four red-zone touchdowns this year, three have come through the air. If the Titans are set on allowing Ward to have this season to hash out his issues - as expected - he'll need to be given a chance to do so in important situations.
In a contest with the Texans likely to yield opportunities for both offenses, the 0-4 Titans could ask for no better reason to open things up. In red-zone looks, the Titans can't hope for the best on the ground. In Week 5, Daboll and Tennessee have no choice but to scheme for Ward and his weapons if they want to keep up with high-scoring Houston.

title: Commanders Got 7.5 Yards Per Carry From Jacory Croskey-Merritt. Then His Carries Stopped
full_text:
Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt led all Commanders running backs with 82 yards on 11 carries in Washington's 27-27 tie with the New York Giants on Sunday . That doesn't sound odd, but the snap count makes it seem off. Despite the 7.5 yards per carry, Bill didn't see the ball over the final 14:20 of regulation or during overtime.
The interesting part about the running back usage in this game is that Bill led the team with 82 rushing yards despite playing 15 fewer offensive snaps than Rachaad White, the team's alleged third-down back. Now, I already know what you're thinking about White and his receiving ability, but he had one catch for two yards, while Austin Ekeler also had one catch for 15 yards.
Jacory Croskey-Merritt breaks free for a 33-yard TD run! 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/9wfDhRQB9V
The Commanders were driving late in the third quarter (:39) when Bill took off for a 22-yard run. The problem is, his next carry, a one-yard gain at the 14:20 mark in the fourth, would be his last. Washington would go up 27-13 with 11:05 remaining. After Bill's final carry, the running back usage shifted , and the process favored White. From that point on, White got all five remaining running back carries and finished with seven rushes for 18 yards, making the move a highly questionable head-scratcher. Those opportunities included early-down situations, not the obvious passing downs White normally plays. After New York cut the lead to 27-20, White took the first-down carry at Washington's 37 with 7:15 remaining, gaining one yard; after that, the second-down play gave them one more yard, Daniels was sacked on third down, and then Washington punted. So basically, with a seven-point lead, the team moved away from what had been working and tried to get White going, but not in a way that highlighted his abilities that outshine Bill in the passing game, making this running back usage confusing. A guy averaging 7.5 yards per carry shouldn't be put on the shelf after breaking off a 22-yard run.
Then came overtime; White took a first-and-10 handoff at the 7:20 mark, gaining three yards on a possession that ended in a punt. After the Cam Skattebo fumble, Washington drove into scoring territory, and White took his last carry at the 55-second mark, gaining two yards. That was the moment the team should have spiked it and sent the kicking team out. Of course, as the entire sporting world knows, that didn't happen. Now, Dan Quinn has talked about whether they even need one featured running back, instead of using different players depending on what the offense needs. I get the thinking, especially since White brings more experience in pass protection and the receiving game, two areas where Bill is still developing . The problem with that explanation is that Washington wasn't asking White to protect Daniels or catch passes on those late carries. They were handing him the ball, mostly on first down, while the guy averaging 7.5 yards per carry wasn't getting another opportunity. Maybe David Blough saw something in the Giants' defense that he liked with White on the field, or maybe something went down with Croskey-Merritt that we don't know about. Both are possible, but until someone from the coaching staff explains the decision, we're left guessing why Washington went away from its most productive running back. I'm not suggesting Bill needs 25 carries every week, and White and Austin Ekeler certainly have a place in Washington's offense. What I have a hard time understanding is how a running back can be having that much success, get into a situation where a couple of first downs could make all the difference, and then never touch the ball again. Would giving Bill another carry have changed the outcome? Maybe not, but I'd certainly rather find out than watch him standing on the sideline. With San Francisco coming up, it'll be interesting to see whether Blough continues using the same rotation or starts giving more opportunities to the guy who's actually producing. title: Commanders Report Card: A 14-Point Lead Vanishes in Disastrous Giants Tie
full_text:
Washington Commanders fans know a low point when they see one. They'd already had plenty of practice through this regular season's first four weeks in watching a near-endless slew of untimely penalties and called-back highlights, occasionally broken up by the occasional devastating quarterback injury , and that's to say nothing of last year's regression to the mean or the two decades of unimpressive football that preceded the Jayden Daniels era.
Their Week 5 tie to the New York Giants may not go down as the most embarrassing moment in the history of the historic and proud Washington football franchise, but it certainly feels as look-in-the-mirror-worthy as any moment since Daniels took over the on-field ship. Even if they didn't have to walk away with a fourth defeat in five matchups, the key Commanders are already acknowledging how much this draw feels like a blown chance at disrupting the divisional standings.
Dan Quinn says the tie feels like a loss. Says he hasn’t talked to Jayden yet but that the coach needs to “make life easier” for his QB pic.twitter.com/Dq4yreEKjG
This 27-27 finish was the sort of matchup that leaves plenty to ponder in choosing the best path forward, even if a few position groups held up their end of the bargain in spurts. Balancing those meteoric early-game highs with the humiliating lows is tough, but we'll try our best.
How do you evaluate Daniels' first day back? He did everything he was asked and more while adjusting to football with a brace protecting his recently dislocated elbow, but he deserves a fair share of the blame pie for his lack of urgency and awareness in that final tie-clinching disaster.
The Commanders can't get the play off in time and this game ends in a tie pic.twitter.com/WmPp6q5hU0
It's also fair to counter that they never would have been in position to keep their five-game win streak against the Giants going without him, with his 300+ all-purpose yards and two rushing touchdowns pushing Washington to an early 14-point lead. The five sacks didn't help, though he may have shown how tough it'll be to win behind a thrown-together offensive line and battered receiving corps when the defense loses steam.
Anyone attempting to look up Daniels' highlights on X will be instead greeted by a flood of angry Washingtonians and befuddled outsiders reacting to the final 12 seconds as opposed to anything that occurred over the nearly-75 minute sequence that preceded that lapse, and understandably so. Daniels wasn't alone in calling it a rollercoaster finish, but more on the coaching staff's performance later.
After weeks of diminishing returns, Jacory ‘Bill’ Croskey-Merritt re-took the reins as Washington's lead back, rushing for 82 yards on 11 carries to lead all rushers not named Daniels. 7.5 yards per carry is the highest per-game mark he's posted through five weeks, and he was sure to enjoy his first red zone return trip since Week 1 in Philadelphia.
Rachaad White wasn't quite so lucky in his own return to the lineup alongside Daniels, attracting just one target to couple with his eight so-so attempts on the ground. At the very least, Washington's coaching staff remains comfortable leaving it up to the backs to control the occasional series on their own, a strategy that couldn't have worked with some of the running back rotations from the last month.
The receivers were there for Daniels when he needed them, but not as much as they have been in other matchups. With the rushing attack holding its weight against New York's solid front seven, the quarterback's platoon of dynamic, Stefon Diggs-less downfield options successfully leveraged their athleticism and hands to meet Daniels where he needed them.
Though none of the recently returned Terry McLaurin, the still-ascending Antonio Williams , or big play-magnet Treylon Burks scored a touchdown, they remained effective in the clutch, keeping the offense chugging downfield whenever called upon. That threesome converted on nine of the 11 passes thrown their way for 119 yards, clearly separating themselves from the rest of the error-prone wideout reserve pack.
Finally, after weeks of minimal impact from Chig Okonkwo's understudies , the starter drew eyes back to Washington's tight end assortment with his first fully healthy outing as a Commander. He finished with 60 yards, nearly tripling his season total of 21 yards through the first four weeks, when injuries and ineffective usage had bogged him down.
Jayden Daniels and Chig Okonkwo are cooking early. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/dRA9FpRpCi
He glided through defenders, repeatedly opening up the middle of the field and giving Daniels a reliable intermediate threat to dish to, with the legs to continue creating after the catch. That's all that's been asked of him since moving to D.C. over the offseason, and it had to feel cathartic for Okonkwo to finally factor into an early scoring wave.
Besides the pass-catcher, few of Okonkwo's fellow targets attracted much attention downfield. John Bates tried his darndest to get his teammates in position during that soon-to-be-infamous clock expiration, while Ben Sinnott drew a pass-interference call on one of his few routes, so they at least have those memories to cherish, with chances at a win having slipped through the Commanders' fingers.
As handy as it was to welcome Sam Cosmi back into the fold, further sparing Daniels from having to get blocked for by another unproven reserve or unwanted journeyman lineman, their quarterback really could have used better protection in his season debut at home.
Brandon Coleman struggled against the admittedly imposing Giants pass rush, giving up several of the five sacks that Daniels took while holding little ground one-on-one. The false starts and holding penalties didn't help, either.
Josh Conerly Jr., Chris Paul, and center Lucas Patrick didn't allow those same routine pressures, but the offensive line is one of those units that's only as strong as its weakest link. As always, Laremy Tunsil is missed.
That vaunted Commanders defense, courtesy of first-year coordinator Daronte Jones , was nowhere to be found as Washington succumbed to a Jameis Winston-led attack and saw its 14-point lead evaporate. Frankie Luvu's energy and instincts were much appreciated, though usual quarterback pressure accumulators Odafe Oweh and K'Lavon Chaisson disappeared when the going got tough.
Winston, a quarterback known for erratic play, shouldn't have played so smoothly against a unit that is disproportionately solid against the run as they are. If nothing else, up-and-coming star Sonny Styles recorded a game-high 13 tackles along with another deflected pass, continuing his reign of terror as Washington's do-it-all rookie disruptor. If only his unit had the consistency (or legs?) to keep that same momentum up whenever the offense failed to score.
Despite the highlights Rasul Douglas and Amik Robertson totaled, a growing trend amidst the Commanders' new-look cornerbacks, 326 yards against the famously interception-happy Winston, is an indictment . Sure, the pick Robertson snagged went down as an immediately questionable refereeing decision, but soft coverage and a lack of that same aggression on those short-yardage completions let the Giants march back in the fourth quarter.
It was good to see Jeremy Reaves, as aware as he was, flying cross-field to make tackles with Nick Cross still out of commission, as he almost netted an interception of his own late in the game. But to fans' disbelief, Mike Sainristil still squeezed in a few snaps in a limited role and somehow allowed a late touchdown to Malik Nabers in single coverage.
MALIK NABERS COMES UP CLUTCH @NYGvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/FF9Fws8i2n
It seems that every time this unit shows life with their veteran disruptors, they reveal just how far away they are from achieving any series-to-series consistency.

title: Everything Dan Quinn Said After Commanders’ Frustrating Tie With Giants
full_text:
The Washington Commanders had a chance to win Sunday's game against the New York Giants, but were left to deal with a tie after failing to get off a potential game-winning field goal in overtime . Head coach Dan Quinn took responsibility for the outcome while also addressing the defense's struggles and Jayden Daniels' performance in his return. Here's everything Quinn said following the game.
Opening statement “Let’s get rolling. With the team, I thought this was a hard-fought game to the wire. Leaving tonight with a tie feels like a loss. And the last sequence, we throw it out of bounds, we clock it, you give yourself a chance to kick it. We pride ourselves on those moments at the end of the game. After the first-down run, still trying to gain more for the kick, the right call is honestly we can go clock it early and don’t put ourselves in that spot. That is my responsibility, nobody else’s. I’m gutted for our team. We were given a lot of opportunities tonight to go find our win, all three phases, and we did not seize them. I thought Payne had an incredible play in overtime, the forced fumble to give ourselves a chance to go back the other way. But like I said, finding a way to nail that moment of that play, we have to do that 100 out of 100 times. And so that falls on me.” Was Jayden just supposed to throw the ball away out of bounds on that play? “Yeah, the sequencing of that does not fall on him. It’s an outside throw or a clock. Those are the two, an out-of-bounds throw or a clock. And that has to come from me. I don’t have to put him into that spot. I can do that earlier and we can finish the kick early. We don’t need to gain more yards. So that’s on me.” Why not just spike the ball? “No, we’re just trying to gain more. We don’t need to. It’s easy enough to say, ‘Hey man, let’s clock it right here. We’re early enough. Go get it.’” Was Jayden aware that there were no timeouts left? “[Opening words unclear.] But like I said, that falls on me, Nikki. He executes what we need to do, and I don’t need to put him in that space at all. This is how we’ve got to go down. We don’t need to gain more. Let’s go win it right here.” “Just frustrated. I’m gutted for our team, and that’s the hardest part. Like I said, leaving tonight with a loss — I mean, with a tie feels like a loss. We had plenty of chances to do things to have a lead and get it into overtime. That’s a whole other discussion, but having the awareness, I thought he made some incredible plays and showed why he is so unique. But at the end, I can make life easy there. Man, go get it. Hit it.” Dan, you get Jayden from the start to the end of the game. Overall, how did you think he played? “Yeah, it was awesome to have him back on the field. The small things that won’t show up, Barry, on the stat sheet, is him at the line of scrimmage killing a run from one direction to another versus a blitz. Him demonstrating the ability to use his legs when he needs to and not forcing that. So those are a few of the things. And then when it gets into the crunch-time moments, you look at Terry, deliver the ball in the right location, and same thing to [name unclear]. So I thought for somebody that’s missed time, I thought he played sharp.” Dan, the defense only allowed about six points through most of the third quarter, and then three straight drives of touchdowns. It’s kind of similar to last week where you limited the Colts and then they scored at the end. Without watching the tape already, what’s your sense of why there was a collapse again this week? “Yeah, we have dug in hard on the response, and there was a number early on, a penalty or something that took us out, to go answer on the response. And as it got more into, they’re down two and hurrying up, that’s the spot that we’ve got to go close it out. It wasn’t the early half of first-, second-down running plays, passes. [Portion unclear.] So having the ability to not allow them to scramble to make the plays, that’s a big deal. And at tight end and receiver, they’ve got premium players, but we have to be able to answer and shut that down. No question about it.”
Dan, how surprised are you about the penalties after the game you just had in London? “Yeah, I want to go and look to find. I want to make sure the pre-snap ones that were early are getting corrected. That was the top of the pile for me to find it. But until I watch them, I can’t give you my assessment of that yet.” You guys had a bunch of injuries, especially in the secondary. How did you think you were able to overcome that to maybe hide some potential weaknesses with guys out? “Yeah, going into the week, it was challenging from an injury standpoint when we got back late and then going into Monday of who would be available, what that would look like. And I thought the team did a really good job of knowing who may or may not be available at receiver and safety. [Answer cuts off in the YouTube transcript.]” How frustrating is it that you couldn’t execute that situation after preparing for it? “Yeah, 10 out of 10. 10 out of 10. And that falls on me, Dave. I’ve got to make sure, as much as we hit it, we’ve got to hit it more. It stings today bad because you don’t get those moments back. Here’s a game that’s going the other way, and we’ve got a chance to flip the script. So I want to make sure that’s a scar that has to be permanent, making sure this is a situation, a scenario that would never present itself again.” Kind of going off Dave’s question there, if it’s something that you guys have drilled and you are prepared, Jayden Daniels stood up there and said that as much. How do you fix that in practice? “More of it. Honestly, that’s the space to go back to. We track every situation that we do. We do them in walkthroughs. We do them in practice. We do two-minute every week. So we’ll continue to do that. The results for today weren’t what I was looking for at the end of the game, and we’ll dig into that as hard as we can. But the responsibility is mine alone to make sure our team’s ready to go.” Dan, just watching that end of the game and the clock ticking down, what’s going through your head in that moment? “Well, knowing that we don’t have timeouts, I’m wanting just to get the ball clocked. And so as the time’s going down, it’s not a good feeling knowing that this moment’s going to be slipping through our fingers.” I did want to ask about the Amik Robertson pass interference at the goal line. I don’t know what you thought of it live or if you’ve had a chance to look at it, but certainly a big call. “Haven’t had a chance to look at it yet. It was a big call, but I haven’t had a chance to view it yet.” Dan, obviously the defense has struggled in the second half of games. You guys were up two touchdowns late in the game. I know everybody’s talking about what happened at the end of overtime, but what role did the defense in the second half play in how this game got away from you guys? “Significant role in the fourth quarter. No question about it. You want to see us respond, even when, okay, it’s within one score, go answer, shut the door and try to get ourselves into a four-minute mode. I do recognize how hard the guys battled, even toward the last play, to say, ‘Okay, this is desperation time to get the ball out.’ But to not have the ability to close it down, that’s what you have to do. You have to go shut the door in that spot, and we did not.” Dan, as you mentioned, while this goes down as a tie, there’s an emotional weight with this game that makes it feel like a loss, particularly given how it happened. How does the team move forward from this? “We will. They’ve been through a lot already in five games, and the locker room, this is a tough team. Having gone through adversity in these games, it doesn’t make it any better, but they are equipped to absolutely dig in and get rolling. Our practices of what we want to do to get ready, they’ve shown a lot of resilience. Those are the ones we’ve had to…

title: Commanders and Eagles Let Cowboys Off the Hook | Around the NFC East
full_text:
Week 5 has come and gone without a single division win: Dallas lost Thursday, the Eagles lost the early game to the Jags, and the Giants and Commanders tied. That said, let's dive right into this week's postgame information.
Recap #TBvsDAL on tonight’s Game Night presented by @ATT . 📺: Up Next ➡️ #DALvsGB 10/18 on NBC https://t.co/VWBCKuIzuH
"Extraordinarily, extraordinarily disappointed," owner Jerry Jones said of the loss, via the team’s official website. "You really do need to get it done when it's there to take. They basically were very physical. I thought both their fronts, was really surprised at how well they ran the ball, how they ran it between the tackles. That was surprising. We thought if they were going to run it, they'd do it outside, and thought we'd put it on the quarterback’s shoulders. Their staff, their quarterback, all their players got a great victory here tonight, and it was a tough loss for us."
Week 5 started brutally for the Dallas Cowboys as they lost embarrassingly to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday Night Football. That dropped them to 2-3 on the season, and considering how poorly they performed on both sides of the ball, that loss was especially deflating. Hope felt lost, but that changed a bit on Sunday. The Cowboys didn't play during the weekend , but things really went their way, as every other team in the NFC East had a game to forget.
Dallas Cowboys fans remember a time when Trevon Diggs was one of the better cornerbacks in the league as recently as 2021. In 2026, Diggs, now a member of the Seattle Seahawks, is not only viewed as a depth piece, but he is also being openly mocked by players who are supposed to fear him. In Seattle's matchup against the San Francisco 49ers, Diggs tried to talk trash with future Hall of Fame receiver Mike Evans. Rather than simply yell back, Evans grabbed Diggs' jersey and turned him around to get a look at the name of the player who had the audacity to start something.
The division nobody wants to win: 1. New York Giants -- 3-1-1 2.Philadelphia Eagles -- 2-3 3.Dallas Cowboys -- 2-3 4.Washington Commanders -- 1-3-1 pic.twitter.com/VBjOh3L9tR
On one end of the blade, Skattebo’s powerful rushing style helped him accumulate 59 yards on the ground for New York, including a 19-yard run that helped the offense approach field-goal range during its second possession in overtime.
Ordinarily we would think of a New York Giants - Washington Commanders matchup as a contest for positioning in the top 10 of the next NFL Draft. This season, though, has looked different. After the Dallas Cowboys’ face plant against previously winless Tampa Bay, and with the Eagles’ core talent level increasingly suspect after retirements, trades, and injuries to key players and three consecutive losses, Giants-Commanders suddenly looked like a game with possible NFC East title implications. On second thought, after watching these two teams play Alphonse and Gaston in overtime, maybe the NFL will decide to ban all NFC East teams from the playoffs. What did we learn from this unbelievable, ridiculous 27-27 tie?
The Giants wound up tying the Commanders at 27, after Washington coach Dan Quinn blew the end of overtime by letting the clock run out before his team could attempt a game-winning 42-yard field goal.
Ngakoue, 31, last played in the NFL in 2024, when he suited up for six games with the New England Patriots after joining the team following his release by the Baltimore Ravens in November. During his stint in Foxborough, he registered nine total tackles. In all, he compiled 14 tackles and 1.5 sacks in 11 games that season.
Jameis Winston’s day started shaky, with 7-of-16 completions for 72 yards and no touchdowns. In the second half, he went 21 of 28 for 211 yards and three touchdowns, with his completion percentage improving by leaps and bounds each quarter.

Philadelphia went up 17-16 with eight seconds left thanks to a 48-yard Jake Elliott field goal, delivering what appeared to be an uplifting win for a team that lost a pair of starting offensive linemen in Lane Johnson (retirement) and Cam Jurgens (trade) this past week and was dealing with a long list of injuries. But on the ensuing kickoff, the Eagles kicked the ball to Ameer Abdullah, keeping it in play instead of trying for the touchback. Say what you want about all the injuries the Eagles have endured this season, but it's been their offense’s inability to do anything – nothing, really - in the second half that has led to this losing streak. "You can't make it up," quarterback Trevor Lawrence said of Hamilton's role Sunday. "It's crazy." Hamilton, one of the NFL's best nose tackles, long-snapped Sunday after All-Pro long snapper Ross Matiscik sustained a first-quarter shoulder injury. "Whatever I can do, do it to help our team," Hamilton said. Hamilton snapped eight times Sunday, including on kicker Cam Little's 57-yard game-winning field goal as time expired. "I wasn't that nervous for that one," Hamilton said. "It just is what it is, got to do a job, get it done. Head Coach Liam Coen said Hamilton, who also snapped for Matiscik in a road victory over the Tennessee Titans last season, practices long snapping "a few snaps a week, maybe" – doing so mostly in walkthrough situations. "It's not in a live setting," Coen said, adding of Hamilton, "We trust him to do it." Said Hamilton, "Hopefully, I don't have to do it next week and we can move on. But it was fun."

title: 5 Winners, 5 Losers From the Commanders’ Baffling 27–27 Tie With the Giants
full_text:
The Washington Commanders led the New York Giants 12-3 at halftime and 27-13 with 11:05 left . The Giants scored two fourth-quarter touchdowns to force overtime. The game's final play was a comedy of errors as the team reached the Giants’ 24-yard line, but time expired before a field-goal attempt. Washington is now 1-3-1 as they will face the undefeated San Francisco 49ers on Monday Night Football in Week 6.
Jayden Daniels’ playmaking Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels was back to his old self, going 17-of-25 for 199 yards and no turnovers, along with nine carries for 103 yards and two touchdowns.  Daniels is the first QB with multiple 25+ yard rushing touchdowns in the same game since Michael Vick in Week 13, 2002, vs. the Vikings. Daniels' runs went for 38 and 26 yards, and the second touchdown and ensuing two-point conversion established the 14-point lead. Jacory “Bill” Croskey-Merritt Croskey-Merritt gave Washington something it hasn't gotten nearly enough of from its running backs through the first month of the season, finishing with 82 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries. His 7.5 yards per carry were impressive enough, but it was how he got those yards that made the difference. On Washington's opening possession, Croskey-Merritt broke loose for a 33-yard touchdown run that gave the Commanders an early lead. He wasn't finished making plays, either, adding a 22-yard run late in the third quarter that helped get another touchdown drive going. We've spent plenty of time discussing Washington's problems running the football this season, and for good reason. Croskey-Merritt finally gave the offense some explosive production from the position, and it's difficult to look at what he did against New York without wondering why Washington hasn't gotten more of that through the first five games. Chig Okonkwo After a disappointing injury-filled first month, Okonkwo finally gave Washington something to work with in the passing game, catching four of his six targets for 60 yards. His first three receptions went for 11, 23, and 25 yards., which is exactly the kind of production the Commanders were hoping to get when they added him to the tight end room. The problem is that all four of his catches came before halftime, and he wasn't able to build on that production in the second half. Still, considering how little Washington has gotten out of its tight ends as receivers this season, Okonkwo's first-half performance was a welcome change. Now they need to find a way to get that kind of production for an entire game. Terry McLaurin McLaurin returned to the lineup and reminded everyone how important he is to Washington's offense, catching all four of his targets for a team-leading 62 yards. It wasn't a huge afternoon statistically, but several of his catches came when the Commanders needed somebody to make a play. He caught the two-point conversion that put Washington ahead 27-13, then added a 22-yard reception to open the team's final possession of regulation. When the Commanders got the ball back for their last opportunity in overtime, McLaurin was there again with a 16-yard catch to get things moving. With the injuries Washington has dealt with at receiver, having McLaurin back gives Daniels a dependable option in situations where he needs somebody to make a catch. McLaurin did his part Sunday, even if the Commanders couldn't turn those late opportunities into a win. Daron Payne and the Takeaway Makers Washington's defense certainly deserves plenty of criticism for what happened in the second half, but there were still players making the kinds of plays that should've helped the Commanders win this game. Daron Payne finished with a 13-yard sack and forced a fumble by Cam Skattebo in overtime, with Shy Tuttle recovering the football to give Washington possession with 1:55 remaining. Earlier in the game, K'Lavon Chaisson recorded a strip-sack that Tim Settle recovered at the Giants' 28-yard line, putting the Commanders in excellent field position. The first takeaway resulted in a field goal, while the second gave Washington the opportunity to end the game with a win. Neither produced the result the defense would've wanted, but that's not on the players who created those opportunities in the first place.
Dan Quinn and the Overtime Operation This one is pretty difficult to explain away, and Quinn didn't try to do that after the game. Washington had the football with 1:55 remaining in overtime after Payne forced the fumble, and the Commanders worked their way into position to attempt a game-winning field goal. Unfortunately, they never actually got around to kicking it. The Commanders had already used both of their overtime timeouts before getting the ball back. With 55 seconds remaining, Rachaad White ran for two yards to the Giants' 24, leaving Washington facing second-and-eight. The next snap didn't come until there were 12 seconds left, and Daniels was credited with a zero-yard sack as the clock eventually expired without another play being run. That's a pretty terrible way to finish a football game when you have a chance to win it. Quinn made it clear afterward that the responsibility belonged to him, not Daniels. "The sequencing of that, um, does not fall on him," Quinn said. "It's an outside throw or a clock. You know, those are the two, you know, out-of-bounds throw or a clock. And, um, that has to come from me. I don't have to put him into that spot. I can do that earlier. And, uh, we can finish, you know, the kick early. We don't need to gain more yards. So, that's on me." Taking responsibility is one thing, but Washington still had a chance to win a game it had already allowed to slip away, and poor clock management kept the Commanders from even attempting the field goal. There's no way Quinn doesn't belong on the losing side of this one. Daronte Jones' Second-Half Defense For the second time in three weeks, Washington's defense couldn't get out of its own way in the second half, and this time it cost the Commanders a win. The Giants had just 77 yards of total offense and three points at halftime, which should've put Washington in an excellent position to finish the game. Instead, Jameis Winston completed 21 of 28 second-half passes for 211 yards and three touchdowns, and New York scored touchdowns on three consecutive possessions. Isaiah Likely's second touchdown came on fourth-and-eight, which is the kind of play a defense simply has to stop when trying to protect a lead. Then Malik Nabers caught the tying touchdown with 1:43 remaining, completing a comeback that never should've gotten that far. New York also finished three-for-three in the red zone, another indication of just how little resistance Washington provided once the Giants started moving the football. Quinn acknowledged afterward that the defense had a significant role in what happened during the fourth quarter. "You have to go shut the door in that spot, and we did not," Quinn said. The defense deserves credit for forcing the turnover in overtime, but that doesn't erase everything that happened before it. Jones has been trying to get his unit to finish games since the season started, and five games in, Washington is still having the same problems. Pass Protection Daniels made plenty of plays with his legs Sunday, but some of that scrambling came because Washington couldn't keep the Giants out of the backfield. New York finished with five sacks, including the zero-yard sack on the final overtime play. Dru Phillips had two, while Abdul Carter and Arvell Reese also got to Daniels during the game. The protection problems became particularly costly when Washington was trying to finish things off, with Phillips recording a fourth-quarter sack that helped force a three-and-out after the Giants had cut the lead to seven. Reese also came up with a sack during Washington's final possession of regulation, another opportunity where the Commanders had a chance to do something and couldn't keep the…

title: Commanders Blow 14-Point Lead, Then Botch Final Chance Against Giants | Game Pulse
full_text:
FINAL: Commanders 27, Giants 27 (OT) The Washington Commanders are back home Sunday to face the New York Giants , back on track, looking to get their season moving in the right direction after last week's 30-13 loss to the Indianapolis Colts dropped them to 1-3. The biggest news for Washington is the return of Jayden Daniels , after missing the last two games with a dislocated elbow. Daniels will wear a brace on his left arm, and with rain and wind expected at Northwest Stadium, his first game back could bring a few challenges beyond just getting comfortable on the field again. One important update from today's inactive lists: Terry McLaurin is active , along with Sam Cosmi and Rachaad White. Stefon Diggs and Marcus Mariota are out. Commanders Game Pulse tracked the action throughout the game, with a full check-in after each quarter. You can also see the full game feed at the bottom of this page, including play-by-play updates and social posts during the game.
- A lot to unpack from this game, but first thing: Daniels was great in his first game back, beyond the brainfart that he and Dan Quinn had at the end. Never is it acceptable to have a game in that situation and not come away with at least an attempt at a FG. - Dan Quinn is feeling the heat tonight, and judging by the lack of positive emotion on his face, he likely has no clue how to deal with it.
- Washington was able to answer New York driving down and kicking a field goal with a five-play, 77-yard drive that ended with a 38-yard run by quarterback Jayden Daniels, where he hit 20.58 mph and left Giants rookie LB Arvelle Reese in his dust. - Seems like every time John Harbaugh uses J.J. McCarthy, it turns out the opposite way he wants. My guess is they are using McCarthy as they would have Jaxson Dart; the problem is McCarthy doesn't have the same skill set. Harbaugh likes a mobile QB, and McCarthy fits that somewhat, just not as effectively as Dart. - Washington has stepped up their defensive intensity; these guys are aggressive up front, on the edges, and in the secondary. The problem, of course, is that Isaiah Likely and Malik Nabers are almost unstoppable.
- Pre-snap penalties have been a killer in this game. Dan Quinn has clearly been irked by them and said the team would work to eliminate them this week. So far, the Commanders have struggled overall in the penalty department, with five for 35 yards. - The first half seemed like the team was playing ultra-conservative, which is somewhat understandable considering the injury situations they've been going through. I expected more play-action, which Washington got back to in the second quarter, but to get the running game going like they want, that is the way. - The defense has looked really good in small stretches. The second half should focus more on making Winston turn the ball over. He's way too problematic not to exploit between the moments he lights up the stat column.
- Washington came out hot throwing the ball to tight end Chig Okonkwo, but had cooled off by the end of the quarter. That needs to be a major part of this team's game plan moving forward. - The offense is coming out and pistol formation a little too much for my liking as the they run things best through play-action passes that doing things under center helps more. Will have to watch that as the game moves forward. - Daniels was noticeably less "jerky" trying to escape and gave in on the sack to protect himself, which was smart.
- The big question coming into this game, beyond Terry Mclaurin's health, has been what will change in Jayden Daniels' game now that he has to wear a brace on his left elbow. Washington's staff has made it sound like that answer is: not much. - The weather will play a factor in this game; not sure how much yet, but with it being Daniels' first game back after dislocating his elbow, I'd expect the staff to be all over him the moment he comes off the field. McLaurin has hamstring issues, and things could shift at any moment.

The Washington Commanders weren't finished making roster moves ahead of Sunday's game against the New York Giants. Saturday brought some help back to the defensive line, another option at receiver, and two players who won't be available after all. New York also made a few moves of its own, while Washington still has some problems to figure out before kickoff. Commanders Make Several Roster Moves Before Giants Game The Commanders announced several roster moves Saturday, beginning with the activation of defensive end Deatrich Wise Jr. from the Reserve/PUP list. Wise was also removed from the injury report, giving Washington another defensive lineman to work with against New York. Linebacker Austin Keys was signed to the active roster, while safety Darren Hall and receiver Van Jefferson were elevated from the practice squad. Jefferson's elevation is particularly interesting with Stefon Diggs already ruled out and Terry McLaurin questionable with a hamstring injury. Washington also downgraded cornerback Trey Amos and running back Jeremy McNichols to OUT, ending any possibility of either making his return Sunday. UPDATE: Terry McLaurin will play. Giants Place Chauncey Golston on Injured Reserve New York had some roster business of its own, placing defensive lineman Chauncey Golston on injured reserve with a neck injury. Golston had already been ruled out against Washington, but the move means the Giants will be without him beyond Sunday. New York also elevated receiver Dalen Cambre and outside linebacker Trace Ford from its practice squad. Washington Has an Opportunity on Third Down Here's something worth watching Sunday. Washington's offense ranks 30th in the NFL on third down, converting just 31.6% of its opportunities, while the Giants' defense also ranks 30th, allowing opponents to convert 48.9%. That's an opportunity the Commanders have to take advantage of, especially with Jayden Daniels returning. His ability to extend plays gives Washington another option, although missing Diggs and potentially McLaurin certainly doesn't make the job any easier. Penalties Remain a Problem for Washington Dan Quinn has talked plenty about discipline and execution, but Washington has committed 30 accepted penalties for 224 yards through four games, and the problem hasn't gotten better. The Commanders have repeatedly put themselves in difficult situations with pre-snap mistakes, and doing that against an aggressive Giants defense could make an already difficult offensive situation even worse. Commanders Prepare for Crucial Catch Game Sunday's game will also feature the NFL's Crucial Catch initiative, which focuses on cancer awareness and early detection. The Commanders published a story featuring Charles Omenihu, Treylon Burks, and Javontae Jean-Baptiste, with all three discussing how cancer has affected people close to them . It's worth taking a few minutes to read their stories.

title: 10 Commanders Quotes That Define Washington Entering Week 5 vs. Giants
full_text:
The Washington Commanders are back home for Week 5 , and there's plenty riding on Sunday's matchup with the New York Giants. Jayden Daniels is returning, the injuries continue to pile up, and Washington has some things to clean up after last week's loss in London. Here are 10 quotes from this week's press conferences that help explain where the Commanders stand heading into this NFC East matchup.
Question: “Morning, David. It looks like the Giants have been able to limit tight ends in their previous four games, outside of maybe Trey McBride. What have you seen from what they’re doing to specifically take tight ends out?” “It’s man coverage. It’s safeties coming down out of the sky wanting to create matchups, and guys have to go out and win one-on-ones. That’s what they’ve wanted to create. It’s a good scheme. They’ve done a good job over there implementing it through the first four weeks, and we’ve got a good challenge on our hands with them coming to town this week.”
Question: “You’ve managed to get the ball to Terry and to Diggs and to Williams, and so has Marcus. Do you think it’s an issue that the tight ends haven’t been as involved yet? Do you think there’s a way to incorporate them into the game plan more, or is it just the guy who’s open gets the ball?” “The guy that’s open gets the ball. We’ve dealt with a lot of different injuries and stuff like that up to this point, where people are in and out of the lineup. And obviously, I think teams do a good job of covering our tight ends, too. So these other guys one-on-one outside, they win too. But we’re just out here playing point guard, trying to get the ball to the open guy.”
Question: “And with Mikey, what do you need to see from him to get back on the field, to kind of earn his way back on there? And how has he handled this rough stretch?” “Mike’s a pro. Mike has been a pro with that. Going into the game plan last week was a little different. It was more so, it wasn’t like keeping him off. We went from a regular personnel, so our true three linebackers against their 11 personnel on the early downs, and then when they got to got-to situations, we went to Big Nickel, which is where Mikey came onto the field. They just were in that 11 personnel early down more than that, and that’s where Kain Medrano was there on those situations. But Mikey as a whole, he understands his consistency and just doing the routine things routinely. He’s working on that day in, day out, and he has a great attitude towards that approach.”
Question: “For you guys, the second-half defense has not been there. The numbers are what they are. Why have there been struggles there in the second half?” “We’ve addressed that with our guys this week and just talking about our ability to sustain, which comes with, we say physical conditioning precedes all else. With that being said, you may be asked going into a game and say, ‘I’m only scheduled to play 25 snaps,’ and end up playing 40. We can’t let that be a determining factor. We can’t let things out of our control be a determining factor. So our ability to respond, our ability to sustain not only success but adversity as well, is building the mental toughness for that. That’s been the focus this week, just tapping into the mental toughness however it may shape and not letting anything outside of what we can control affect our play. And then also focus. I think a focus, play in, play out. We talk about, you don’t have to be great and locked in for 70 plays. Just have to be locked in and great, or damn good, for one play 70 times, and that way you can take one play at a time.”
Question: On the Giants' defense and what kind of game Washington expects Sunday. “Yeah, it is definitely a trenches game on both sides. I thought Dennard’s done a nice job with their unit. They’ve got speed out on the edges. They’ve got big guys inside, linebacker play. I’ve been impressed by what I’ve seen from them. As you’re going back and forth, different packages, run game premium for sure on both sides. Classic line-of-scrimmage football day. Might be some good football weather as well. Even if it’s not, we’re still going to have a line-of-scrimmage game.”
Question: “Speaking of a guy who likes to give advice, Jameis Winston is someone who has historically turned the ball over a lot. How does your approach change, if at all, when you know there’s a guy who is prone to giving up interceptions?” “Well, that same guy is also prone to making big plays. He’s done that in his career, which is why, obviously, it’s not a one-way street with Jameis. Jameis is a guy who is high risk, high reward, and because of his reward and the plays that he’s made in his profession is why he’s still doing the things he’s doing now, especially for the New York Giants and why they’re where they are right now is because of a lot of him and providing those opportunities. We can’t be mindful of, yeah, he’s going to turn the ball over. He can also put four or five touchdowns on you in a heartbeat, which I’ve experienced that back at the Bengals, back at the Dolphins, and even with the Vikings when he came in with the Saints when Derek Carr got injured. So his strength is his ability to one snap and clear. That’s dangerous for an opponent because whether it’s a great play, he can move on. Whether it’s a bad play, he can move on. Each play has a life and history of its own, and he’s the true definition of that. So you’ve got to be mindful of that.”
Question: “With regard to the offensive penalties that you’re having, I know you want to have some continuity, but you do have the power to remove people from the field if they continue to make those mistakes. Is that something that you consider doing?” “I would definitely consider that. And I’m certain that we are going to get this fixed. Certain. We have to. There’s no ifs, ands or buts about it. Losing big plays due to a pre-snap foul, and in the defensive case a post-snap foul, cost us. We’re going to work really hard to attack that.”
Question: “Along those lines, is that what you mean when you say this one’s different? Just the fact that you’ve gone through what this process is like, or is it something else that feels different?” “I mean, yeah, I went through the process and it wasn’t the end of everything. Like I said, I was blessed enough to still be allowed to play this game, and I’m just going to go out there. I’m going to embrace it. I’m going to embrace the brace. Not really worry too much about it and go out there and just be the best version of myself.”
Question: “You have a quarterback like Jayden coming back after the dislocation and he’s coming back wearing the brace. How does that affect your game plan in any way, knowing maybe what he may or may not still be able to fully do, or is he full-go and you can game plan without limitations?” “He’s full-go, man. We’re looking forward to having him back.”
